Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law

Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison

The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.

In his ruling on Thursday, the high ​court judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.

He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.

Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.

Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.

After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy. The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”

Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”

Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats was also present for the sentencing.

The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.

The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.

Shortly afterwards, China warned against “irresponsible” remarks on Hong Kong’s judicial affairs. “Relevant parties should earnestly respect China’s sovereignty, respect Hong Kong’s legal system, stop making irresponsible remarks regarding the trial of … judicial cases,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told reporters.

Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine under the headline: “The face of protest.”

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.

Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law.

stories.title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
stories.summary: Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.

Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.

One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects.

In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.

Most notably, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor race that Axios reported would fundamentally scramble the math on Trump’s AI buildout. According to Bloomberg , Hinojosa’s election has developers facing down the “worst-case scenario.” Texas is the epicenter of the AI boom, Axios noted, and was expected to account for more than 41 percent of added data center capacity in 2028.

Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects as long as it takes to pass laws “tackling impacts on water, electricity, air, and property rights.” Approximately “13 gigawatts of data center capacity” is now exposed, Bloomberg reported. Gordon Johnson of GLJ Research warned in a note that Texas projects with “power, permits and steel keep going,” but “those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months,” Bloomberg reported. Some projects may leave the state entirely, perhaps moving to Louisiana or Georgia—or perhaps going nowhere.

“She would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills, and ends the tax incentives for data centers,” Johnson’s note said. “The question now is how long the pause lasts.” As PIMCO head of public policy Libby Cantrill similarly warned, “even if statewide moratoria do not result, we expect to see a lot more sand in the gears of the AI buildout regardless—with more time required to secure permits and other approvals, as well as more concessions that data center developers will have to make.”

Big Tech downplays AI election results

Texas wasn’t the only big shake-up. Democrats won governor races in the next three biggest states previously wooing data center developers—Arizona, Georgia, and Ohio. Overall, Axios projected that “nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity” could face similar delays as Hinojosa threatens in Texas. Bloomberg estimated that half the data centers in the US are now more vulnerable to scrutiny.

For AI firms, that’s a nightmare, since any delays will set back revenue, and IT consulting firm Gartner recently estimated “the AI boom is nearly $5 trillion short of paying for itself.”

Likely soon, developers nationwide will face tighter rules limiting tax incentives and requiring stronger protections for residents around who pays for grid infrastructure and water use. Those kinds of regulations will most likely increase developers’ costs at an inconvenient time, Bloomberg’s report said.

While many reports suggested that the first so-called “AI election” proved the power of the people to rein in Big Tech, some AI industry insiders downplayed the election results on Wednesday. In a statement, Adam Kovacevich—a former Google executive and the CEO of a tech industry trade group and policy coalition called Chamber of Progress—suggested “the results offer little evidence of a voter mandate to crack down on AI or data centers.” He emphasized that “Democratic gubernatorial candidates who opposed data center bans won at a higher rate than those who supported them,” and admonished, “Let’s not confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate.”

“Voters wanted change on the economy, not a crackdown on innovation,” Kovacevich said, while sharing a resource for those in the tech industry seeking an alternative spin on the results.

Poll: 3 out of 4 voters opposed data centers

NBC News exit polls suggest it’s true that issues like cost of living or government corruption were ranked as more significant by voters than AI and data centers. However, like many analysts who point to AI opposition as a make-or-break issue for many voters, Alejandra Montoya-Boyer, vice president of The Leadership Conference’s Center for Civil Rights and Technology, disagreed with Kovacevich’s lens.

“The 2026 midterms have been the first true AI election in the US,” Montoya-Boyer said. “We saw voters turn up at the polls in record midterm numbers and vote for leaders who are willing to protect them and their rights from unchecked AI.”

Montoya-Boyer cited NBC’s polls showing that 3 in 4 voters are opposed to data centers. Additionally, more than half of voters said that “AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.” The mass backlash is not just about utility costs or other data center fears, Montoya-Boyer suggested, but instead stemmed from a call from voters to regulate AI. Election day came “as the biggest AI companies raced to go public, AI systems broke out of the test ‘sandboxes’ meant to contain them, and biased and discriminatory AI kept making life-altering decisions about us,” Montoya-Boyer said.

“These results confirm numerous polls and what we civil rights leaders have been hearing from the communities we represent: Innovation is only real when it includes all of us and actually improves our lives,” Montoya-Boyer said.

Other analysts told Axios that voters appeared to be “more concerned about efforts to block state AI regulation than they are about data center controversies,” with one noting that across four swing districts, “voters trust Democrats over Republicans to hold AI executives accountable by a margin of 7 to 10 points.” Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios that “voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers.”

“What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake,” Carson said.

Expert: China benefits from US slowdown

Slowing down America’s AI infrastructure buildout could hamper frontier AI and set the US back in the so-called “AI race.” That’s Trump’s main rationale for refusing to regulate the AI industry.

Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at a global financial institute called the Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, told the South China Morning Post that “a slowdown in the US could be a win for China.”

Like analysts who projected that Democrats won’t try to block all data center development, Ng suggested that the AI buildout won’t come to a complete halt following the “blue wave” unseating many Republicans. However, a Democrat-controlled Congress will likely “introduce new constraints on US computing capacity,” and that could give China a leg up, Ng suggested.

“This would keep [US] AI token prices high, giving China an opportunity to export cost-effective inference services, supported by abundant electricity supplies,” Ng said.

At the furthest extreme, US data center opposition could push giants like Amazon or Google to build hyperscalers outside the US, Ng suggested. That outcome represents the opposite of Trump’s vision for 100 percent US-made tech , which experts have warned is an impossible dream.

Michael Strobaek, global chief investment officer at Swiss private bank Lombard Odier, noted that Trump still has the power to veto any federal laws that Congress may advance. Democrats will likely need “substantial Republican support” to pass laws over a potential veto, Time reported . However, with a majority, Democrats could threaten to block Trump’s efforts to roll back Environmental Protection Agency protections to aid data centers, according to some analysts.

Musk among election day’s biggest losers

On Wednesday, Trump did not directly mention AI in a batch of Truth Social posts reacting to election results. Instead, he seemed to blame Fox News for hosting Democrats, while arguing that outcomes would somehow have been different if he was on the ballot.

But Trump’s silence suggests that he has no talking points to gloss over the fact that polling from Blue Rose Research showed that “Americans would rather live near a prison, methadone clinic, or a nuclear power plant than an AI data center.” And while existential fears that AI firms like Anthropic have recently warned about are a concern for many Americans, “concrete local impacts” like higher energy bills or pollution “were far more salient” for voters, Blue Rose’s director of research, Ali Mortell, told Time. And even when developers promise to cover costs, “trust in institutions is low,” to the point where even “when tech companies and politicians offer reassurance,” Mortell said, “voters are not positioned to believe that’s true.”

“There’s not a clear divide between Democratic voters and Republican voters on how they’re thinking about [data centers],” Mortell said. “Opinion has soured with everyone.”

Counting among the biggest losers on Election Day was Elon Musk, who is currently facing a lawsuit over allegations that the gas turbines at his Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, are emitting pollution. Musk dumped “almost half a billion dollars” into Republican candidates as of October, “a sum no other individual donor in the 2026 midterms approaches,” Quartz reported .

The SpaceXAI founder had joined other tech CEOs and AI SuperPACs in donating “hundreds of millions in campaign contributions to guard against any meaningful federal regulation,” Montoya-Boyer said. But “voters proved unswayable,” and instead elected members to Congress who vowed to probe AI firms.

As the votes came in, SpaceX and Tesla shares dropped , as investors perhaps questioned if a potential merger between those firms may now be in doubt, with Musk’s political foes back in power and in a position to add friction.

With opposition possibly mounting, Musk appears to be immune to the pressure and determined to plow ahead with expanding his controversial data center on a much faster timeline. According to SemiAnalysis , an independent research newsletter covering the AI industry, SpaceX recently revised its estimate for the data center capacity it’s building out for 2027. Instead of aiming to reach 10 gigawatts of capacity, SpaceX notched its goal up to approximately 13GW in 2027.

“This would be the largest amount of data center capacity ever built by any one company in that timeframe, roughly equivalent to all of Google’s data center capacity from 1999-2026 in just 1.5 years,” SemiAnalysis reported. “We think it’s possible and have already identified more than 9GW of capacity.”

stories.title: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
stories.summary: Job, loans and savings are all affected by the rise in interest rates announced by the Bank of England.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 November 2026, 12:02 GMT

Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you.

Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you.

1. Jobs and pay

Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level.

Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.

This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up.

Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate.

Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises.

Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.

That could include greater use of robots rather than workers.

"It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said.

"You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further."

2. Boost to savings

The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products.

So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news.

When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too.

The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates.

What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages? Published 1 day ago

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it Published 28 September

Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty.

"Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.

She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative.

The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords.

3. Mortgages and loans

The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages.

About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.

Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost is going up by about £31 a month now the Bank has raised the base rate, but it depends on the size of people's loans.

An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) must wait to see if their lender chooses to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.

If you, like 87% of mortgage-holders, have a fixed-rate deal, then the payments will stay the same until the end of your current deal, which is usually two or five years.

While monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, future deals are. Lenders had already "priced in" the latest rate rise when quoting new deals. Expectations for the Bank rate into next year are crucial on what they offer next.

The average rate on fixed deals are much higher now than was predicted at the start of the year. It means those remortgaging, possibly after the post-Covid boom in the housing market, are facing the prospect of higher mortgage payments.

Some people have been choosing to move onto tracker deals instead, taking a view - including some risk - of the Bank rate not moving towards a series of further hikes.

In today’s newsletter: From the cost of living to the AI bubble and the fight against fascism, Weber answers Guardian readers’ questions on how to build a fairer economy and world

G ood morning. As stateside celebrations die down, the Democratic party will be forced to confront a (deceptively) simple question: now what? Their colossal midterm successes will curtail Trump’s power during his remaining time in office, but the battle to shape the Democratic platform heading into next year’s presidential primaries is only just getting started.

While rallying against Trump is one thing, sustaining support by making a tangible difference to the lives of voters struggling with the cost of living is another. It’s a challenge for progressive parties facing down the far right across the world.

For years, economist Isabella Weber has argued that progressive politicians can win back voters by focusing on a fundamental issue: make life’s necessities – housing, transport, food, water, energy, healthcare – affordable to all. It’s the basis of her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics , and her ideas have found a receptive audience in New York, where Zohran Mamdani, who has followed Weber’s work for years, has made affordability central to his agenda. Now, a raft of progressive candidates have won on similar platforms . Weber’s influence is also being felt in the UK, with Andy Burnham’s Labour conference speech echoing much of her messaging.

A few weeks ago, we asked you to send in questions for Weber. In today’s First Edition, she answers them. That’s after this morning’s headlines.

Five big stories

UK | Cocaine has overtaken heroin as the biggest cause of drug deaths in England and Wales, figures from the Office for National Statistics show.

France | Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in demonstrations across France as trade unions call for a nationwide strike expected to extend to hospital workers, air traffic control, the post office, teachers and rail staff.

Commonwealth summit | The UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year with Caribbean nations affected by the slave trade and its legacy, Commonwealth leaders have said.

US news | Pete Hegseth is increasingly looking like he may take the fall for Republicans’ midterm losses, despite Donald Trump’s vocal support for his defense secretary, even calling him a champion of war.

Ebola | A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

Isabella Weber answers your questions

What are the most interesting or radical actions governments are taking to improve affordability in an increasingly volatile world? Jack in Ireland

IW: Mexico’s government has an agreement with grocery companies to fix the price of a basket of essential foods. President Claudia Sheinbaum is making clear that it is her responsibility to negotiate on behalf of ordinary people and make essentials affordable. This is the opposite of neoliberalism, which tells people that democracy is the greatest system, yet that elected officials can do little to meet their basic material needs. Mexico has also capped energy prices, guaranteed small-scale farmers minimum prices for staples to encourage domestic production, and built emergency buffer stocks.

Spain capped the price of gas for power generation, which effectively contained the 2022 energy shock, offered free commuter and regional rail passes while the crisis lasted, and established public scrutiny of corporate profits.

At the municipal level, Vienna stands out : around half of its residents live in municipal or subsidised housing. Istanbul has pioneered people’s canteens that offer nutritious meals at an affordable price point. And New York City has put affordability policies such as rent freezes, investment in housing stock and public supermarkets back on the international agenda.

﹡﹡﹡

How should these midterm results shape Democratic economic policies? Should they be cautious or bold? Jessica in Brighton, UK

The Democrats won votes on affordability , and now they must have the courage to deliver real change. A dignified life for all must be the north star and that requires a fundamental overhaul of the economic playbook. Last time the Democrats enjoyed an electoral wave was in 2008, and under Obama they then leaned into neoliberalism. Bidenomics got stuck in a halfway house.

This time, the economy needs to be rebuilt starting from the essentials – energy, food, housing, communication, transport, all forms of care – with investments that create meaningful and decent jobs. Short term measures such as price policies can buy time and build power to regain public control over the essentials on which our lives and industries depend. We must then change how we provide them so that provision is compatible with planetary boundaries while constraining corporate power.

﹡﹡﹡

Why do governments use interest rates to control inflation? It seems unfair and clumsy. Simon in Perth, Australia and James in Leeds, UK

We often say interest rate hikes cool down the labour market – it sounds nice, like a fresh breeze. But simply put, the goal of rate hikes is to curb inflation by increasing unemployment and weakening workers’ ability to demand high wages. Higher rates also raise the cost of investments, for example in renewable energy that would make our economies less vulnerable to future shocks, and they increase mortgage costs, deepening the housing affordability crisis. This causes considerable harm, potentially pushing people towards the far right.

That is why I argue for surgical, sectoral stabilisation policies for essentials that buy time for structural measures. Rate hikes remain the standard response, whatever the nature of inflation, because central banks are in charge of monetary stability and have only one instrument at their disposal. We need a new approach in which governments fight inflation too, and central banks take on new tasks such as monitoring profit margins and issuing early warnings about rising prices of essentials that can unleash inflation.

﹡﹡﹡

Why do economists accept 2 to 3% inflation as OK but not 0%? Wouldn’t consumers be better off if prices went down rather than up? Rich in Michigan, USA

The 2% target is an arbitrary rule of thumb for central banks, established relatively recently. But the idea that a little inflation supports steady growth is old. If purchasing power slowly declines, there is an incentive to invest or spend rather than hoard cash in your mattress. Moderate inflation also makes debt servicing easier, both for private borrowers and governments.

﹡﹡﹡

Why are we obsessed with economic ‘growth’? It seems to drive self-destructive behaviour. Richard in Hampshire, UK and Tim in Lewes, UK

This is a live debate, especially in the context of climate change. Capitalist economies are predicated on growth because capital always strives for greater profits, but growth does not automatically guarantee a dignified life. What I am arguing for is to replace this growth imperative with an affordability and full- employment imperative: essentials should be removed from profit fundamentalism and organised to ensure affordable provisioning for all, and the government should be responsible for guaranteeing decent and meaningful jobs.

﹡﹡﹡

I support a vigorous tax on wealth. Something like a 100% tax on all wealth over $1 b n. Do you agree? Bill in Virginia, USA

Roosevelt warned that “the liberty of a democracy is not safe if private power grows stronger than the democratic state itself: That, in its essence, is fascism-ownership of government by an individual, by a group, or by any other controlling private power.” This was a key lesson from the consolidation of the Nazis’ power. Taxing the ultra-rich to limit extreme wealth concentration is key to anti-fascist economics. A 100% tax on wealth over $1bn might, however, not be the best design. A progressive tax that limits wealth accumulation starting at somewhat lower levels would make it harder to amass a billion dollars to begin with.

﹡﹡﹡

What will happen if the AI bubble bursts? Fiona in Edinburgh, UK

The immediate impact would probably be a stock market crash and a financial crisis. But such a crisis would also present an opportunity to turn things around. Governments should not bail out the companies but socialise them and turn them into democratically controlled utilities.

AI has cannibalised humanity’s knowledge and automated it to make profits for a handful of companies that openly state their business could lead to human extinction; it should serve the common good instead. As it creeps into our work and we increasingly rely on it in our daily lives, we will have to take public control of AI while also creating space for knowledge creation and creativity that are not competing with AI services. Otherwise, exercising the mind will become a privilege of the wealthy few. Some questions have been condensed for clarity.

after newsletter promotion

What else we’ve been reading

Having recently finished reading Yesteryear, I find myself perhaps more fascinated by trad wives than I’d like to be. Lucy Knight’s deep dive into the women leaving the movement, was excellent and eye opening. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

I love Coco Khan’s writing, so I made a beeline for her column on why celebrities wear tone-deaf Halloween costumes . In it, she unpicks “the strange, insulated life that comes with sustained wealth”, while being very funny and somehow, against all odds, hopeful?! Genius. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

There are so many ways to put together a stunning portrait. I loved looking at this year’s gallery from the Winston Taylor Portrait Prize – call me basic, but my favourite is the six-year-old Elvis impersonator. Poppy

Our interview with Kathryn Hunter was heartbreaking and brave, done excellently by the warm and brilliant Paula Cocozza . Poppy

I am not one of those admirable souls who gets their Christmas shopping sorted with weeks to spare. But having realised there’s nothing in this gift guide that someone in my life wouldn’t love, I feel this could be the year I’m done and dusted by mid-November. Lucinda

Sport

Football | Liverpool surrendered their 100% Champions League record, losing 3-2 at Fenerbahce despite leading twice, while Arsenal held on to win 2-1 in Czechia.

Rugby union | The Six Nations and Sanzaar unions have agreed to sell all their media rights and commercial deals collectively for the first time in a new revenue-sharing model.

Golf | Rory McIlroy voiced his support on Wednesday for the DP World Tour chief executive’s claim that LIV Golf’s goal was to “destroy” the European golf circuit.

The front pages

“Trumped”, is the Guardian ’s front page headline today, while the FT goes with “Crushing midterm rebuke to Trump”, and the Times writes “Trump faces backlash as Democrats make history. The Telegraph writes “Vance turns on Trump”, similarly The i Paper has “Vance blames Trump’s war for crushing defeat”, and the Mail says “Maga turns on Trump”. The Mirror ’s headline is “Reborn in the U.S.A.”, and Metro writes “Lame Donald Duck”.

Elsewhere, the Express , on asylum seeker housing, has “You are not listening!” and the Sun leads on “Markle ‘filth stash No3’”.

The Latest

Democrats’ midterms triumph deals devastating blow to Trump’s Republicans

Democrats have won a historic sweep in the US midterm elections, winning back control of Congress in a major setback for Donald Trump. Senate seats went blue in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas – which saw the first Democrat win since 1932. Voters have sent a strong message of discontent to the Trump administration over the economy, the cost of living and rising gas prices. Trump is now a lame duck president for the rest of his term as president. Lucy Hough speaks to Washington editor Ankita Rao.

Cartoon of the day | Martin Rowson

The Upside

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Phoebe Waller-Bridge, the creator of the hit show Fleabag, has bought and donated a London flat to Writers’ Block – a scheme tackling class barriers in theatre – so that early-career writers can live in the capital rent-free while they attend meetings, rehearsals, and other career opportunities.

Other high-profile creatives backing the scheme, which invites Londoners to offer spare rooms to writers at reduced rates, include Jack Thorne, who co-created Adolescence, and James Graham, who wrote the stage show Dear England.

“When I first made it to London, I slept on friends’ floors and worked in call centres … while I wrote,” says Graham. “Every spare room a scheme like this can give to writers starting out in London, not only helps them write but saves them from giving up completely.”

Bangers and rockets light up the skies as the winter nights close in

Published 14 minutes ago

Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.

The government is currently considering reducing the limit for the noisiest fireworks for private use by 50%, after pressure from campaigners concerned about the impact on nervous animals and people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).

About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, according to industry figures.

Andy Hubble, of the British Fireworks Association, said displays had already been getting quieter and a balance must be struck to prevent a black market in noisy fireworks springing up.

The end of October sees the start of several celebrations traditionally marked by fireworks and bonfires, including Halloween on 31 October, Guy Fawkes Night on 5 November, and Diwali, which is on 8 November this year.

The government has said an outright ban on the public buying fireworks would not be proportionate.

But Business Minister Kate Dearden said her department was considering "reforms to fireworks legislation, focused on their key harms associated with their misuse - their noise, and contribution to antisocial behaviour – whilst still allowing individuals to enjoy fireworks safely and responsibly for the important community and cultural celebrations they play a part of."

It is already illegal to sell fireworks to under 18s, or to set fireworks off after 23:00, with exemptions for special occasions including Bonfire Night, Diwali, New Year's Eve and Chinese New Year.

But campaigners have raised concerns about the impact of loud bangs on nervous pets.

Dog owner Katherine Alderson, from Clacton-on-Sea told BBC Breakfast: "It's a nightmare every single year.

"This year I've actually barricaded my bedroom window with numerous layers of insulation to try and keep out the noise of fireworks."

Asked whether reducing the bangs would take he fun out of fireworks, she said she believed displays "should be about the lights and colours" and suggested "a complete ban" the sale of fireworks to the general public could be the solution.

A woman enjoys fireworks in a crown of people

But other groups say a ban is not needed, included Alan Friggieri, from the charity Combat Stress, which supports veterans with PTSD.

Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons' Business Committee, Mr Friggieri said calls to their helpline jump at this time of year because loud bangs can trigger PTSD symptoms.

"Nothing quite sounds like an AK47 other than fireworks going off - it's that crackle," one veteran who had been shot multiple times had told him.

Mr Friggieri said veterans need to be able to plan around key dates, but he said he was not calling for a ban, because his organisation understands the cultural importance of firework displays.

Calling for better enforcement of existing rules by police to stop antisocial behaviour, British Fireworks Association (BFA) vice chairman Mr Hubble warned a ban in Ireland had seen a flourishing black market in firework sales.

"There is a real risk here that if we make fireworks quieter that there is still a demand then we could create an illegal market where fireworks are coming in through internet sales and white van sales," he told BBC Breakfast.

"At the moment we have a really well-regulated market where we have enforcers that know the products and can test them but as soon as these products go undercover then we lose that.

"We could actually create a louder and noisier environment because those are the sorts of fireworks that we're seeing coming in through illegal sales on the internet."

Asked whether it was true that displays were getting noisier, Mr Hubble said: "No, no, it's a lot quieter than it used to be - we used to have bangers and air bombs and and screamer rockets that used to be on sale and they were withdrawn from sale."

Mr Hubble said a BFA assessment of firework sales shows a 50% noise reduction to 110 decibels, which is what the government are considering, would impact up to 60% of firework sales to the general public.

Lowering levels to 90DB would affect about 95% of fireworks.

"That's effectively a ban on consumer fireworks, not a modest reduction in noise," he said.

RSPCA advice for people with nervous pets:

Stay calm and show your pet that all is well

Put on music or the TV to help mask firework sounds

Close any windows and do what you can to block out both the noise and the flashes

Keep your environment secure: make sure your pet can't escape if there's a sudden noise

For dogs: let them pace around, if they're whining, barking or hiding, let them

Play with a toy if your pet wants to join in, but don't force them to play

Combat Stress advice for people with PTSD:

Use noise cancelling headphones to reduce the sound of explosions and blackout blinds to block out flashes of light

Use scented candles, diffusers or plug ins to make your home smell good and nothing like those you remember from deployments

Remind yourself you are safe, and focus on the present using breathing and grounding techniques, or with exercise

Ask friends and family to be with you on key dates like Bonfire Night

stories.title: Ted Cruz aims to stack FCC with Republicans before Democrats take Senate control
stories.summary: Cruz and Trump seem to have no plans to fill FCC's empty Democratic seat.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Cruz and Trump seem to have no plans to fill FCC’s empty Democratic seat.

Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is aiming to widen the Republican majority on the Federal Communications Commission before Democrats take over control of the Senate in January 2027.

Just before the Republicans’ midterm loss, Cruz yesterday announced a November 10 nomination hearing for Trump’s FCC nominee, Danielle Thumann Severs. In his final two months as chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, Cruz seems set on moving the Thumann Severs nomination to a full vote of the Senate.

Confirming Thumann Severs would give Republicans an unusual 3-1 advantage on the FCC. That could become a 3-0 advantage at the end of 2027 because FCC Democrat Anna Gomez would have to leave the commission at that time if Trump does not agree to renominate her.

Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) recently warned that federal law prohibits an all-Republican FCC and that “any action taken by a partisan FCC could be overturned in court, based on the statutory history of the Communications Act.” Wyden wrote in a September 24 letter to Gomez, “Because the Communications Act sets a quorum at three members, there is speculation that the President intends to fire you once [Thumann Severs] is confirmed, attempting to run the agency with an all-Republican 3-0 panel.”

“Under an all-Republican commission, every single license renewal, equipment certification, spectrum transfer, or other delegated action would be legally defective, casting a cloud of crippling legal uncertainty over the entire communications industry,” Wyden wrote.

Trump hasn’t nominated a Democrat

Every FCC commissioner must be nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. By tradition, the president nominates opposing-party commissioners based on recommendations from the opposing party’s Senate leaders.

The bipartisan process has ensured that the FCC’s makeup complies with US law, but Trump hasn’t followed the tradition in his second term. He has failed to nominate a Democrat to the other empty FCC seat and has not renominated Gomez so she can continue past 2027.

Gomez today issued a statement calling on Congress to fill the empty FCC seats in a bipartisan manner.

“We must rebuild public trust in the FCC by returning the public interest standard to its original meaning as an obligation to communities rather than a tool for political pressure,” Gomez said. “That means defending the First Amendment and a free press from government interference, advancing competitive innovation that smartly protects our communications networks, and delivering real results for consumers.”

Thumann Severs is an attorney and senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Trump nominated Thumann Severs in August , but a Senate nomination hearing originally scheduled in September was postponed to accommodate her maternity leave. We asked Cruz’s office about plans for Thumann Severs’ confirmation vote and will update this article if we get a response.

Maintaining a quorum

The Communications Act requires the FCC to have three members for a quorum. The US law also forbids supermajorities on the FCC by specifying that “the maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”

In previous administrations, the president and Senate agreed on paired nominations to ensure that the president’s party maintained a 3-2 advantage. Senate Democrats have been pushing for the Thumann Severs nomination to be paired with a new Democratic nominee so the commission can have a full slate of five members. When it became clear that wouldn’t happen, Democrats asked Trump to at least renominate Gomez in order to maintain a 3-1 split.

Twenty-one Democratic lawmakers on the House Commerce Committee wrote a letter last week to Cruz and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), urging “that any new Republican nominee to the commission be paired with the nomination of a qualified Democratic commissioner, including the renomination of Commissioner Anna M. Gomez to a full term.”

The letter continued:

The Communications Act limits how many commissioners may belong to one political party, ensuring that decisions on broadband, media ownership, and network security are tested by more than one point of view… Robust disagreement, independent judgment, and deliberation strengthen the commission’s decision-making and provide an important check when the FCC considers policies with far-reaching implications for consumers, competition, and constitutional freedoms.

Gomez’s voice of opposition

Gomez can’t prevent any major regulatory actions that Carr’s majority is set on taking, but she has been a consistent voice opposing Carr’s attacks on Trump’s least favorite news organizations and attempts to police speech on broadcast TV . She also has occasionally convinced Carr to make changes to rulemakings that she argued would harm telecom consumers.

The Democrats’ letter said Gomez has been a strong advocate for telecom consumer protections, competition, network security, and access to affordable high-speed broadband. “Additionally, the FCC’s licensing and enforcement authority over broadcasters carries real constitutional limits, and Commissioner Gomez has taken that seriously, defending editorial independence and speaking out when she believed that authority was being stretched beyond its proper role,” Democrats wrote.

Gomez’s term technically expired on June 30. US law allows her to serve until the end of 2027 or until the Senate confirms a replacement, whichever comes first. Severs would not replace Gomez because Trump nominated Thumann Severs to fill a different seat in a term expiring in 2029.

If the Senate confirms Thumann Severs during the lame-duck session, it would be reminiscent of the December 2020 confirmation of Trump nominee Nathan Simington. The vote, taken shortly after Biden’s 2020 election win over Trump, resulted in a 2-2 deadlock at the start of Biden’s term. The Biden-era FCC remained deadlocked at 2-2 until Gomez was confirmed by the Senate in September 2023 .

stories.body:
Yesterday, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Ninth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Spurlock , a case involving a “tower dump” warrant. These overbroad warrants require cellular providers to turn over location data about every phone in a given area at a given time. This is the first such case to be heard by a federal appeals court since the US Supreme Court ruled this summer that highly similar “geofence” warrants are searches under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

Spurlock involves an investigation into two murder victims discovered on the side of a rural California highway. Police also found a car belonging to one of the victims several miles away on the same highway. They quickly sought a tower dump warrant for an area covering this stretch of road, which eventually revealed location data on nearly 1,700 unique phones. Faced with a motion to suppress, the district court relied on a Fifth Circuit court of appeals decision about geofence warrants to hold that tower dumps are similarly categorically unconstitutional “general warrants” that violate the Fourth Amendment. However, the court refused to suppress evidence on the basis of the “good faith doctrine.”

Our amicus brief on appeal makes several key arguments.

First, we point out that the Supreme Court’s decision in the geofence case Chatrie v. United States this summer only strengthens the arguments that tower dumps are unconstitutional general warrants. Tower dumps are a somewhat older technique than geofence warrants, but they are both “reverse location searches,” in which police “tap into an all-encompassing database, allowing them to undertake nearly perfect, retrospective surveillance of countless persons and places.” This is the sort of untargeted “general warrant” the framers of the Fourth Amendment wanted to prevent. As we write in the brief, “Searching all people in an area without probable cause to believe they were all involved in the criminal activity under investigation reproduces the evils of general warrants and is not constitutionally permitted.” It’s this rule of law that prevents police from searching the houses of a hundred, or even a thousand people in the vicinity of a crime.

Second, we note that even if high courts continue to allow tower dump and geofence warrants in any cases, core Fourth Amendment law requires strict limits to protect the privacy of innocent bystanders, including limits on the scope and duration of the warrants, as well notice to affected individuals and after-the-fact deletion and minimization of irrelevant data.

Finally, we argue that the Fourth Amendment requires the court to set aside the good faith doctrine in cases like these and actually decide the constitutional issue. Too often courts pass the buck in cases involving novel surveillance techniques, leading to situations where police can continue using the technique for years or even decades without a definitive ruling.

Exclusive: pro-democracy activist’s prison letters reveal fascination with AI, brushes with Triads and an appetite for books

Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case

F rom inside Hong Kong’s oldest maximum security prison, where he swaps books with Triad gang members and studies law, Joshua Wong writes letters like a man desperate to stay connected to the outside world.

Excerpts from his private prison writings reveal the pro-democracy activist asking friends to take screenshots of social media accounts and put questions to AI chatbots on his behalf.

To one acquaintance, he writes about his prison reading habits. “Some of the old-school triad bosses in here have also lent me books,” he says in the letters to friends, seen exclusively by the Guardian. “They read too. One of them lent me Mario Puzo’s The Godfather (lol).”

The 30-year-old Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s now-squashed democracy movement, has been imprisoned since November 2020.

On Thursday, he was sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion , his second conviction under the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020. Wong pleaded guilty to the charge in September.

Wong is the only pro-democracy activist to be prosecuted twice under the national security legislation. He had been due to be released in January, before the latest prosecution, and will now serve his two sentences concurrently.

Despite spending his 21st, 25th and 30th birthdays in prison, Wong’s letters – written between August and October – show his resolve and continuing concern about Hong Kong’s future.

“The only thing I worry about is that people will forget Hong Kong, and that amid competition and struggles between great powers, they will forget the countless ordinary, unknown people in different places who have paid a price for their beliefs,” he writes.

In Stanley prison, where young inmates use M&Ms as currency, he spends time exercising, learning to play the guitar and teaching English to other prisoners.

“I was teaching English to a Russian,” he says in one letter. “When he asked me what the word ‘totalitarian’ meant, I simply answered, ‘Putin’ (lol)”.

Books appear to be central to his life. His reading list includes Patriot, the memoir of Russian opposition leader, Alexei Navalny, who died in prison in 2024; biographies of Steve Jobs, Nelson Mandela, Benjamin Franklin; and the memoir of former Citibank trader turned YouTuber and inequality campaigner, Gary Stevenson.

On the day of the US presidential election in November 2024, he watched votes come in while holding a copy of JD Vance’s bestselling memoir, Hillbilly Elegy.

Wong gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared – with his trademark black-rimmed spectacles – on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

In 2020, Beijing said its introduction of the national security law was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics said it gave authorities sweeping powers to crack down on free speech and dissent.

Since then, activists and journalists have been arrested, independent newsrooms closed, and much of the city’s political opposition forced into exile . There have been more than 400 arrests under national security legislation, according to Hong Kong’s security bureau.

“Joshua’s case is part of an attempt to control how my generation’s political history is remembered,” says Frances Hui, a childhood friend and pro-democracy activist in exile.

“For years, people around the world could hear him argue, organise, and explain what he thought Hong Kong’s future should be. Now we can barely hear from him at all.”

In his letters, Wong says Mandela inspired him to study law and he has enrolled in an undergraduate company law course.

He says that he has lost weight, but has a strict routine of pull-ups, squats and pushups. He also reads the Bible and recites passages from the book of Joshua and the Corinthians.

Wong’s childhood friends and fellow activists say the Hong Kong they once fought for no longer exists.

“It is hard to say whose side time is on,” says another childhood friend, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.

Hui says that Hong Kong authorities had waited nearly five years after the alleged crime to prosecute Wong – just before his release.

“By the time he sees freedom, he is most certainly not going to be the young boy we once remembered,” she says.

stories.summary: A consultation will consider fines and other ways to clamp down on dangerous e-bike riders.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 hours ago

People riding drunk or dangerously on e-bikes – and those who jump red lights - could face on-the-spot fines under plans to curb anti-social behaviour.

Firms which run shared e-bike schemes will also be expected to manage their fleets better and provide designated parking areas to keep pavements safe.

They could also be required to take out insurance so people can claim compensation if they are hit by someone on a shared bike.

It's part of a crackdown on what ministers called the "wild west" of e-biking – with a patchwork of rules across the country often leaving the streets unsafe for pedestrians.

A consultation launched on Thursday sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.

The first e-bikes were launched in Exeter in 2016 and arrived in London a year later, growing to become a popular commuter option.

According to the Greater London Authority, 37 million trips were taken on dockless e-bikes last year – a third more than the previous year.

Shared e-bikes - such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt - make short journeys quick and convenient.

While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes can only be left in specific areas, others have looser rules.

Under the government's proposals, local leaders will be able to license schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks.

Measures could include requiring operators to have a parking plan and to manage fleet sizes and operating areas, so bikes aren't overcrowding streets.

The consultation will also consider ways to tackle antisocial and illegal behaviour, to prevent users from riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements. There will also be clear consequences set out – such as fines for this type of behaviour.

The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the e-bike clampdown was a "small but important everyday fix" which would make streets safer.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the changes would "stop nuisance parking, tackle antisocial behaviour and make journeys safer".

Bosses at Lime, Voi and Bolt all welcomed the proposals, adding that consistent standards being applied across the country would provide clarity and certainty for operators, riders and the general public.

stories.title: Google Summaries Aren't About AI, They're About Lock-In
stories.summary: Whether they call it AI summaries, knowledge panels, or AMP, Google takes actions that are less about functionality and more about locking you into its own ecosystem. Knowing that makes it possible for all of us to choose better services than Google's, defeating their anticompetitive goal. In this case, as it is so often, knowledge is power. In the old days, when dinosaurs roamed the earth and getting online involved your computer making eldritch shrieking, Google was a website that took whatever you typed in and gave you a list of links that best matched what you were searching for. As it's grown beyond that, however, the core function of Google Search has moved from giving you the best answer to your query to a number of other things, most of them about making money for Google. This is obviously not a new observation. It's at the core of what EFF Special Advisor Cory Doctorow named " enshittification ." But it's important to remember that whatever shiny new name or technology is wrapped around these tools, it's not about the wrapping, it's about the monetization. In the case of Google Search, the company has a history of rolling out new "features" that are less helpful to the searcher and more designed to keep you and your data within the Google ecosystem. One easy example of enshittification is putting sponsored links and ads at the top of search results, forcing you to scroll down past a bunch of not relevant links to get to your answers. Or, in some cases, accidentally clicking on sponsored links that might be designed to give you the opposite information of what you're looking for or for a competitor to the product you intended to buy. The other clumsy version of this is Google's self-preferencing, where Google's own services—say YouTube if you're looking for a video—are weighted so that they appear at the top of a search over a competitor's. Similar to this was Google's push for websites, particularly news ones, to be made available via what it called "Accelerated Mobile Pages" or AMP , which in theory stripped out features that might make loading a page on mobile too slow, but also handed over control of how webpages looked on mobile to Google and turned mobile links, often by default, into Google links. stories.body:
Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base

Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.

Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an affordability crisis , particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters believed the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.

It’s hard to ignore the impact inflation has had on this election. Key voters had expressed for months deep discontent with what had become the status quo. Loggers in Maine said that tariffs against Canada were hurting their already-battered industry. Drivers in Texas facing three-hour commutes to work were spending $400 a month on gas. Farmers across the midwest said diesel prices were exacerbating a growing season beleaguered by drought.

Recent data showed the flip wasn’t just seen among Democrats and independents, who have held pessimistic views on the economy since Trump returned to office, but among some Republicans, too.

In February, right before the war in Iran began, 49% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By October, that number would drop to just 28%.

The pain seemed especially acute for rural voters, long considered a core base for Trump.

The president had gained many of his supporters by angling himself as a successful businessman who would be an outsider in Washington. But soaring gas and diesel prices have been a major pain point in parts of the country where driving long distances is an everyday part of life.

Rural voters were much more likely to say that gas prices were hurting their finances and that they were in economic “survival mode”, or that one surprise bill could sink them, compared with their urban and suburban counterparts. They were also slightly more likely to say that Republicans had a bigger problem with corruption, or elected officials using their position for personal financial gain, than Democrats.

In the month before the midterms, the number of rural Americans who said the economy was getting worse climbed 17% since Trump took office, compared with a 5% increase for those in the suburbs and a 3% jump among urban voters.

Yet on the eve of the midterm elections, Trump was trying to speak a different reality into existence, one where gas prices were going down, wages were rising and the US’s trade with other countries had never been stronger.

“I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks, and America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote,” Trump said in front of the Lincoln Memorial’s reflecting pool on Monday. “I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

But the reality that Americans have been facing is vastly different, and Americans responded accordingly. Republicans in key races from Maine to Texas lost their toss-up races on Tuesday, and Democrats will have control of Congress for the next two years.

Democrats have promised they will be busy trying to address the issues that were at the forefront of the election: the Trump administration’s brutal immigration crackdown, corruption in the White House, rising healthcare costs and the economy, specifically higher prices.

Republicans are just starting to take stock of the role prices had on the election outcome. JD Vance on Wednesday said the loss was the “cost to pay” for the Iran war. “Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance said.

As much as the midterms were a “blue-nami” for Democrats, pre-midterm polls showed voters were still unsure about the party’s ability to deal with affordability. When asked which party had the solution to the affordability crisis a month before the election, 34% said that neither party had a solution. Democrats (27%) slightly edged out Republicans (24%), but many voters seemed unsure whether any party could deal with these pocketbook issues.

Similar polling conducted before the 2024 presidential election showed that key independent voters were feeling just as pessimistic about the economy. Inflation had reached a generational high in 2022, and many Americans felt that Biden and Democrats weren’t doing enough.

Price increases under Trump, particularly after the Iran war, have only gotten worse. But many voters are dealing with years of economic burnout and will expect results in the coming years.

stories.title: Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats do anything to ease cost of living pressures?
stories.summary: Democrats will hold Congress but President Donald Trump still has the power to block their plans.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
House Democrat leader Hakeem Jeffries said "now it's our job to govern on affordability"

Published 6 hours ago

Two business owners, half a country apart, want the same thing for different reasons.

In Texas, Kim Hanks, who owns Tillies, a hotel, restaurant and spa business near Austin, says rising grocery and fuel costs are forcing her to raise wages for her 300 staff.

"It's been such a moving target for us on affordability," she told the BBC World Service.

In Indiana, Danny Reynolds, who runs Stephenson's of Elkhart, a clothing and bridalwear store, simply wants Washington to get its act together.

"My hope is that we can just find some consistency, some working together," he said.

Democrats say they heard both messages.

"We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability," said House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries on MS Now's Morning Joe.

But here comes the difficult part. Democrats will hold Congress. Donald Trump still has the power to block their plans.

A message that cut through

The scale of the win was bigger than most forecasters expected, with at least seven Republican-held Senate seats changing hands.

Behind the result was a striking mood: just 21% of Americans are satisfied with the direction of the country, even though the economy looks healthy on paper.

Voters weren't looking at the statistics. They were looking at their grocery bills, electricity bills and the price at the petrol pump.

The outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner for Texas Sid Miller says ranchers 'feel betrayed'

In rural Texas, rising costs were even hurting Republicans in their own backyard. Sid Miller, the outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner, told me ranchers are getting $300 to $500 less for each head of cattle, while also facing record fertiliser costs.

"They felt betrayed," he said.

This was more than a blue wave. It was a vote about the cost of living. So what can Democrats actually do about it?

The affordability plan

Under the banner "Fighting for an Affordable America," Democrats say healthcare is their first priority.

They want to bring back the extra financial help that made health insurance cheaper under the Affordable Care Act and reverse the cuts to Medicaid signed by President Trump in 2025.

Next come tariffs and energy. Democrats want to scrap the president's import taxes, which they say add thousands of dollars a year to the cost of groceries, fertiliser and building materials.

They also want to end the war in Iran, which they link to petrol prices averaging $4.18 a gallon, marking an increase of nearly 40%.

Housing is next. Some Democrats want to build four million new homes over the next decade.

On tax, they want to make billionaires pay more and increase tax credits for families with children.

It's a long list. But how much of it can they actually deliver?

What can they actually pass?

Investor Ken Fisher, founder of Fisher Investments, puts it bluntly:

"Congress can't get anything past a presidential veto. President Trump can't get anything he wants."

The result, he says, is likely to be two years of relative quiet on the legislative and regulatory front.

In other words, winning in Congress does not give Democrats a free hand. President Trump can still block legislation, and getting around a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.

Import taxes now account for more than 5% of federal revenue

For voters hoping for lower bills, that may be a disappointing result. They didn't vote for political deadlock.

Take tariffs. Trump is unlikely to abandon a trade policy that is central to his agenda. Democrats will need Republican support if they want to change it.

Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Oxford Economics, expects the average tariff rate on imports to stay around 10% for the rest of Trump's term.

And there's another complication.

Tariffs are bringing in more money for the government. Import taxes accounted for just over 1% of federal revenue in 2024. This year, they account for more than 5%.

That growing contribution to government income, Yaros argues, will make tariffs "tough for a future administration to fully dismantle."

Still, there are bargains to be struck.

What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress Published 18 hours ago

Where the deals might be

President Trump told CNBC he could work with Democrats on "many more things than people understand".

Healthcare might be one of them.

Yaros sees the possibility of a big political trade-off: Democrats agree to extend Republican tax cuts in return for restoring health insurance subsidies. But he doesn't expect a deal until late 2027, with the economic benefits arriving in 2028. That's a long time to wait for anyone struggling with bills today.

Oregon Democrat Ron Wyden, who is set to chair the Finance Committee, says he will seek to "reassert congressional authority" over trade policy

Democrats could also turn up the pressure on businesses.

Henrietta Treyz of consultants Veda Partners says Democrats will question companies that passed on the cost of tariffs to customers.

After the Supreme Court ruling in February, she says, the question will be: "Did you turn around, take that tariff rebate, and then lower prices for consumers?"

Companies will also be asked: "What did you get in exchange?"

Democrats, she adds, will "pick and choose very carefully."

In the Senate, Ron Wyden, the Oregon Democrat set to chair the Finance Committee, has summed up his approach in six words: "affordability for us, accountability for them."

He says he will use the committee to "reassert congressional authority" over trade policy. Insurers, drugmakers and banks should expect to be called to explain themselves.

And some of the biggest changes may happen closer to home. State governors and regulators have a say in electricity prices, while local authorities decide where new homes can be built.

Democrats have won governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where the rising cost of electricity for data centres is already a concern.

The part they can't control

The hardest test may be something Democrats cannot fix with a new law.

The price of petrol, diesel and fertiliser will depend heavily on what happens in the war with Iran. And forecasters disagree about what comes next.

Oxford Economics warns that with the election over, further escalation "appears more likely," because petrol prices will no longer be as much of a political concern for the president.

And here's the awkward part. If prices come down, Democrats may struggle to claim the credit. If they go up, they may share the blame.

There is an immediate test, too. Government funding runs out after 11 December, and the chances of another shutdown look uncomfortably high.

Democrats won the argument. Now they have to show they can make life cheaper.

stories.body:
La demande en peaux d'âne a connu une croissance exponentielle au cours des 15 dernières années, principalement sous l'impulsion de la Chine. Lauren Johnston est spécialiste des échanges commerciaux entre la Chine et l'Afrique. Elle a passé plusieurs années à étudier le commerce des ânes et vient de publier un ouvrage , intitulé China, Africa and the Market for Donkeys (La Chine, l’Afrique et le marché des ânes). Elle répond ici à quelques questions sur ses conclusions.

Qu’est-ce qui motive cette demande ? Quels sont les pays où le marché est le plus important ?

La demande provient presque exclusivement de Chine. Cela s’explique par l’existence d’un remède ancestral de la médecine traditionnelle chinoise appelé ejiao, prononcé « e-jyow », consommé aujourd’hui par des dizaines de millions de Chinoises. L’ejiao est un tonique sanguin fabriqué à partir de gélatine de peau d’âne.

Depuis des millénaires, il est utilisé pour traiter la fatigue, les vertiges, la toux sèche et les saignements irréguliers, ainsi que pour favoriser le bien-être féminin. Pendant la majeure partie de cette période, cet élixir était fabriqué à la main et consommé par un petit cercle d’élites impériales. Ce n’est qu’au cours des dernières décennies que la production a pris une ampleur industrielle.

Je suis économiste plutôt que spécialiste en nutrition, mais d’après ce que j’ai compris, la réputation médicinale de l’ ejiao est liée à sa composition riche en collagène et aux peptides bioactifs produits lors de sa transformation, ainsi qu’aux allégations concernant les propriétés minérales de l’eau utilisée dans sa production . Bien que la recherche pharmacologique ait mis en évidence des propriétés potentiellement bénéfiques , la mesure dans laquelle celles-ci se traduisent par des effets thérapeutiques cliniquement établis reste contestée . Une question plus générale se pose également : des bienfaits comparables pourraient-ils être obtenus à partir de sources alternatives et plus durables de collagène ou de composés apparentés ?

Le marché de l’ ejiao était, jusqu’à récemment, principalement médical. Mon livre détaille la commercialisation très récente – et stupéfiante – de l’ ejiao et sa transformation en une gamme de produits allant des gâteaux et boissons aux cosmétiques et autres produits de bien-être . Si l’ ejiao est vendu à des prix abordables en pharmacie, tant en vente libre que sur ordonnance , il se négocie également à des milliers de renminbis sur le segment haut de gamme du marché . Le principal producteur, Dong'e Ejiao, a été à l'origine de hausses de prix sur le segment haut de gamme, supérieures à celles dont ont bénéficié les propriétaires immobiliers de Shanghai et de Pékin au cours des années 2000 et 2010.

Il existe également une demande à Hong Kong, à Taïwan, aux États-Unis, en Europe, en Australie et en Asie du Sud-Est.

Read more: La demande de la Chine pour les ânes d'Afrique augmente : pourquoi il faut contrôler ce commerce

Quel est le rôle des pays africains en termes d’approvisionnement ?

L’Afrique abrite la plus grande population d’ânes au monde. Lorsque l’industrie de l’ejiao a commencé à manquer de peaux d’ânes vers 2010, le continent est devenu une cible de la chaîne d’approvisionnement, tant légale qu’illicite. L’Éthiopie, le Kenya et la Tanzanie ont été parmi les premières cibles, en raison à la fois de leurs ressources en ânes et de leur proximité géographique avec la Chine. Mais la demande de peaux d’ânes – et les bénéfices qu’elle génère – est devenue si importante qu’aucun âne du continent africain n’était pratiquement plus à l’abri.

Une peau d’âne peut rapporter plus de 400 dollars américains en Chine.

Les ânes sont des animaux de trait en Afrique depuis des millénaires. Le marché est en grande partie informel. Compte tenu du prix que peut atteindre leur peau, les ânes sont vendus alors même que leur travail est essentiel. À cela s’ajoute leur faible taux de reproduction, qui affecte l’offre. Ce cycle aggrave le risque d’extinction.

Des frontières poreuses et éloignées, des réglementations divergentes et une application inégale de celles-ci ont rendu presque impossible l’endiguement de ce commerce. Mon livre détaille l’expérience de la Tanzanie. Le pays a renoncé à tenter de conclure un accord officiel à l’échelle du continent pour mettre fin à ce commerce. Cette décision fait suite à ses frustrations face à la contrebande d’ânes, notamment à la frontière kenyane, à son incapacité à réglementer les chiffres et les normes d’abattage, ainsi qu’à son échec à mettre en place des programmes d’élevage suffisants.

Quelles mesures ont été prises pour mettre un terme aux exportations ? Ont-elles porté leurs fruits ?

La première Conférence panafricaine sur les ânes , qui s’est tenue en 2022, a réuni des représentants du Bureau interafricain des ressources animales de l’Union africaine (UA-IBAR), du gouvernement tanzanien et d’autres représentants gouvernementaux de tout le continent, ainsi que des associations de défense du bien-être des ânes, des groupes de réflexion et des universitaires.

Cet événement a abouti à la Déclaration de Dar es Salaam , qui appelait à un moratoire continental de 15 ans sur l’abattage des ânes pour leur peau. Le 37e Sommet de l’Union africaine, qui s’est tenu en février 2024, a soutenu cet appel et a approuvé ce moratoire. Il s’agissait d’un moment historique pour la protection de la biodiversité africaine et des populations rurales pauvres, en particulier les femmes.

Mais la mise en œuvre s’est avérée imparfaite , car elle nécessite une adaptation des législations de chaque pays membre et une application cohérente de ces lois. Des progrès sont en cours, mais ils sont loin d’être suffisants pour sauver l’âne, sans parler du bien-être des communautés qui comptent sur son travail pour leur mobilité physique et économique.

Interdire le commerce peut le pousser vers la clandestinité et le faire passer par les frontières. Les restrictions imposées par l’Afrique du Sud ont détourné l’approvisionnement vers le Lesotho, où les normes des abattoirs sont moins strictes.

Pourquoi ce commerce pose-t-il problème ?

Tout d’abord, parce que l’offre ne parvient pas à suivre la demande.

La demande actuelle en ejiao nécessite 4 à 5 millions de peaux par an, bien plus que ce que le cheptel d’ânes chinois peut fournir. Les ânes sont connus pour leur faible taux de reproduction. Ce déficit a été comblé par un commerce mal réglementé, s’approvisionnant principalement en Afrique, qui abrite environ les deux tiers des ânes du monde.

En conséquence, les ânes sont souvent volés, privant ainsi les ménages ruraux d’animaux essentiels à leur subsistance. The Donkey Sanctuary, une organisation britannique de défense du bien-être des ânes, estime que la Chine importe plus de trois millions de peaux d’ânes par an, dont 25 % à 35 % proviennent d’animaux volés .

Deuxièmement, la hausse des prix a des conséquences sur les communautés. Les prix des ânes ont grimpé au-delà de ce que les familles pauvres peuvent se permettre. En Afrique du Sud, un âne qui aurait rapporté environ 30 dollars américains à la fin des années 2010 se vendait 125 dollars américains en 2022, lorsque le moratoire a été imposé.

Cela a eu des répercussions sur les moyens de subsistance, en particulier pour les femmes et les filles. Les ânes transportent notamment de l’eau, du bois de chauffage et des produits agricoles dans une grande partie des régions arides et reculées d’Afrique. En posséder un permet aux femmes d’économiser environ cinq heures de travail par semaine et aux enfants au moins une dizaine d’heures. Lorsqu’un âne est volé ou que son prix devient inabordable, les revenus du ménage, la sécurité alimentaire et la scolarisation en pâtissent.

Ce commerce engendre également la peur, la méfiance et les conflits au sein des communautés.

Il a par ailleurs été associé à la criminalité organisée, à des abattages inhumains et à des risques pour la biosécurité .

Qu’espérez-vous que votre livre permette d’accomplir ?

Les lecteurs de cet ouvrage en apprendront autant sur la Chine que sur ce marché atypique des ânes. C’est un prisme à travers lequel on peut comprendre l’économie, l’histoire et le rayonnement mondial de la Chine. Et j’espère que ce récit contribuera à sauver cet animal.
