stories.title: In Praise Of Japan’s Failure To Keep Up
stories.summary: The post In Praise Of Japan’s Failure To Keep Up appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The country was told it needed to be more like Silicon Valley to compete, but its refusal may have left it better placed to decide what technology is actually for.

Journalist and broadcaster Michael Fitzpatrick has run with all the big game of journalism while inhabiting more countries than is absolutely necessary.

TOKYO — Nothing triggers the bog-walloping Fenian in me quite like a visit to the British Embassy. This one, with its fine Georgian-revival facade, looked on my last visit a decade ago like a lost Cotswold manor-house brought to life in Tokyo.

But what was it that I found so unsettling? Perhaps the stately setting? Or its gilt-framed displays of a preternaturally regal, late queen? Her gaze following me about the room as I moved among the fine art and mahogany, like those creepy Sacred Heart of Jesus portraits I grew up with. Me, a lad reared in an Irish republican home where the Queen’s annual Christmas messages were as welcome as a poltergeist.

To the more clubbable, the embassy’s English country house manner would have seemed merely civilized; a demonstration that Merrie England had acquired over generations the ability to arrange the upholstery without the aid of an AI shepherd.

The decor was a projection of centuries of British self-assuredness and ease, distilling, as adroitly as the form allows, the essence of (an ebbing) sovereign power. The fine art, damask and agreeable lighting gave no hint that Britain’s technological might has long migrated elsewhere. That such hegemony now lies with American platforms and Asian supply chains. But the genius of spaces like these is that you can start to believe in a type of fanciful continuity of the imperishable.

It inveigles you into sharing a fantasy. This one being that if these old arrangements had survived war, decolonization, Tamagotchis and the mobile phone, perhaps it might survive the latest digital convulsions, too. Here was a refuge, some autonomy even, from the technological superpowers that increasingly own us. Proof that small jurisdictions of taste, privacy and human-scale abound.

Of course, like any contemporary state, the British must put on a show of modernity. Outside the embassy hung long banners declaring that England was now a “Unicorn Kingdom.” But from where I was standing, the oak heart of this very British establishment demurred. They had seen it all before. But it was co-opting some of Silicon Valley’s grandiose illusions just to be safe. Inside the older, more powerful unicorns of mythology resided sinewy on the royal coat of arms. Not just representing rarity, but purity and extreme ferocity, reminding me of some English public-schoolboys I knew.

But this is the great charm of the embassy interior — its refusal to update. Even in the face of economic realities and the dark, immutable forces that forge them. Here was a stand for the moral and institutional habits of our ancestors.

A Sinking Feeling

Big Tech oligarchs can threaten to transform all that is before them, but the timeless endurance of this lived-in aristocratic grandeur will survive, I was starting to feel. Now I — sinking in someone else’s club chair — was beginning to get it.

Assailed by crypto pirates, the succubi of VC-led extractor corporatism and the crumbling of knowledge work , we feel profoundly the foundations of power shifting ominously beneath us. Countering that are the Embassy’s older, time-tested values and their comforting familiarity. People like the faddish Steve Jobs would probably have hated it. Like death for Californians, he thought furniture was optional.

Beyond the embassy precincts, Japan too was stealing itself from Darwinian upheaval, slouching toward it from across the Pacific. That was 10 years ago. Now the evolution has landed, proposing a shotgun wedding with a prenuptial dubbed Pax Silica.

The vow is simple: Join our techno view of the world or be made irrelevant by it.

Or you can do what the embassy valiantly attempts: indulge in wishful thinking that we are beholden to no one; sovereign power is unassailable and will prevail over any forces that seek to unseat it. Look! We have brass sconces! Damask pelmets!

Eventually, I allowed myself to be consoled, finding one of the ambassador’s snugglers, an oversized armchair, to sink into and reflect. Besides, despite residues of unease, it was too late to bolt. The mayor of London, Boris Johnson at the time, had been promised forth — attended by the nation’s press and its tech somebodies — to expand on a subject without any obvious tripwire: London’s thrusting home-grown cashless tech.

I had a fancy I might know better. As a former hack himself, Johnson knew how to give good copy, and I had an uncharitable thought he would not disappoint.

After all, Johnson had already just snot-o-grammed a schoolboy in a game of mock rugby the day before. Metaphors for the bumbling, bruiser foreigner riding roughshod over finer Japanese sensibilities came tumbling off the press. And why not? We in the geographical West have plenty of form here.

“Japan too was stealing itself from Darwinian upheaval, slouching toward it from across the Pacific. That was 10 years ago.”

Polite rebuffs, coded rebukes, and death threats from Japan aimed at preventing Johnny Foreigner from putting his size-12 welly through the shoji doors have often proved futile over the centuries. We were never much good at taking the hint.

It fell to U.S. Navy Commodore Matthew C. Perry in 1853 to finally dash aside Japan’s isolationist polite “Please Do Not Disturb” sign to demand, with menaces, access rights. Included in the list of “diplomatic” offerings was a white flag, should the Japanese ever feel the need to employ it.

Almost touchingly British, this American politely tapping on the door while carrying a battering ram. And echoing today’s political realities, when faced with “having no cards,” capitulation must follow as night follows day.

Can’t Put A Good Man Down

Now we had a capering politician on a trade mission to Japan for whom such blundering was just a warm-up act. Japan’s wall of unassailable, face-saving etiquette would ensure his next gaffe.

Johnson was on his pins, grandly pitching the City Boys’ latest Fintech triumph — its “light-years ahead” magical, cashless payments tech. The marvelous BRITISH tech in question was contactless IC (integrated circuit) cards, which made paying for travel on the tube absolute duck soup.

Pausing to ask rhetorically, “Who else can boast that?” he practically invited an intervention. And so … apostle of truth that I am, I did not hold back. From the press seats, I pointed out that Japanese travelers were largely already there should they wish it. Japan had had the cashless tech for years, and practically single-handedly conjured up the tech in question while others fumbled for dimes. A couple of years back, I had even completed a journey — with mixed results, I have to say — around Japan to try out humanity’s first tentative steps toward going cashless.

Obviously, no news of this had reached the British capital, or the ears of the mayor’s flunkies, because suddenly Johnson looked all in, spluttering into his cuffs: “Really, is this true!?” A sea of dark heads bobbed in assent.

“Have I just undermined the whole raison d’être of this event? So, what is my raison d’être for being here?” he queried, eyeing his aides. “Why was I not told this?”

Summing up the possibilities, I arrived at a few rapid deductions. Firstly, his immediate staff and the embassy had signally failed to do their homework. Secondly, too many of his hosts were equally bereft of the facts concerning their own country’s digital prowess in this matter.

Third, and most crucially, a naked emperor, no matter how richly deserving of exposure, is still an Emperor in Japan; only on pain of social death should he be confronted with the humiliating truth.

It was an object lesson in the terrifying extremes to which Japan is willing to take its impeccable manners. Selling coals to Newcastle may be ill-advised, but apparently in Japan the correct form is for Newcastle to politely deny the existence of its coal pits in the face of such magnificent British magnanimity.

Yet this gaffe can be forgiven, if only because the Japanese themselves were largely in the dark about their own tech — having long refused to trust anything but hard cash. Because of this typical national recalcitrance, the contactless technology perfected in Japan decades ago initially went nowhere , no matter how hard any Japanese Boris Johnsons tried to push it. It was only after the tech took off in Europe and elsewhere in the 2000s that it gained a widespread local following.

The Root Of All Evil Is Progress

For me, this became a quiet symbol of the failure of progress and of our rightful reluctance to submit unconditionally to its tyranny. A new tyranny that demands societies adapt to every new technology. But as Japan proved, we do not have to. The fact that Japanese innovation remained so entirely invisible, even to the fintech envoys themselves, is also symptomatic of how Japan’s tech research routinely fails to achieve a global impact commensurate with its genius.

What is missing, as is so often the case in Japan, is the aggressive cultural machinery required to turn raw research into a bankable international asset.

The country lacks, above all, the cultural instinct to shout its name from the rooftops. When advised to do so, heads are patiently shaken in agreement, and eventually, it’s determined that no shoestring is too threadbare for the task. Even the most prestigious startup factory at Tokyo University has only one part-time PR rep. She does not speak English.

“What is missing, as is so often the case in Japan, is the aggressive cultural machinery required to turn raw research into a bankable international asset.”

Consequently, there is very little understanding of how global visibility is created.

Treating communications, international business development and storytelling as peripheral administrative functions suggests a genuine contradiction here. Universities are being ordered to create globally competitive companies but seem blind to the fact that they are institutionally unsuited for the task. After observing such behavior time and time again in Japan, the communications gap is glaringly real.

Could such attitudes be an atavistic return to the days when storytellers, entertainers and the like were classified under Japan’s feudal caste system as literally “ hinin ” non-humans?

A suspicion, not unwarranted, that marketing and PR, like all stories, are a kind of … lies. Manipulative ones at that. When I asked about the story from these cloistered university startup hubs, the basic reply was, “Anyway, what use is a mere ‘story’ when you have specs!?”

Was this where Japan was failing startup-wise? I wondered.

Never Losing The Plod

A few years later, I think I heard my answer: “It’s not about the tech, it’s about the execution,” explained one Tokyo tech insider at a startup meeting.

Where Japan often fails, he continued, was the slow pace of business. He was right. Japanese commerce likes to plod, and the Japanese are inveterate plodders. Decisions take months, even years, to kick things around, assess, assess, assess, then slowly “build trust” for the sake of “nemawashi” (preparations).

Japan’s sluggish adoption of cashless payments perfectly illustrated this trend. What was lost on its hapless Japanese inventors and investors was that they alone held the keys and were the legislators and instigators of a powerful new digital tool that the Tech Tyrants across the ocean had failed to monopolize.

Londoners, forever with an eye out for every angle, understood better. Fintech of this ilk being perhaps its only success yet at stemming a tide of American tech dominance, there was much to harumph about. While not a wholly British success story, it was about the only Big Tech triumph the UK could cling to before burlier Fin-Tech Bros sharp-elbowed them back to their country estates.

In the face of it, Japan and the UK seem powerless to stop this leaking away of sovereignty. Japan’s puzzling foot-dragging on the tech illustrates an overlooked aspect of its innovation drive — its long history of brilliant innovations that were, for various reasons, overlooked and sidetracked. It also illustrates very well Japan’s institutional-character problem and its uncanny ability to turn wine into water.

Opportunity Knocks

It was Toyota that ushered me into one of its first commercial electric cars 30 years ago. Ditto, a self-driving vehicle that same year. Thanks to a “mad-scientist dream” for humanoid robots, a Japanese computer scientist told me 15 years ago that her country led the world in AI machine learning. Now, like Japan’s version of the Rip Van Winkle tale, Taro Urashima, the nation is waking up to find it overslept in all these fields.

Its less cautious neighbors, famously, ran with the tech Japan had been quietly pioneering, leaving the country on the wrong side of a technological divide entirely of its own making. The American giants, meanwhile, rose rapidly, ate everyone else’s lunch, pocketed their dinner money and now appear to be talking options on any future breathing plans others may be foolishly having.

That’s why we rant about Amazon, Apple, Meta, and the like as tech’s “Magnificent Seven,” and not the Seven Samurai. Contemporary Japan simply often fails to capitalize on, or communicate, its genius.

China, too, is leaving Japan and the rest of us at the bedroom door. It may have gotten its lead by “distilling” all the best ideas from Japan and elsewhere, but China is now outpacing us with the speed it has put these applications to use.

Ask any savvy Japanese, “How so?” and they’ll evoke the “Galápagos” theory. Like the plants and creatures on those famous islands, Japan’s tech standards and business practices have developed a unique character incompatible with overseas wants and desires.

Even the country’s myriad startups throw up lots of weird and wonderful concepts only seen in Japan, earning them domestic fans but a condemned death march if tempted to ship abroad due to their lack of marketing savvy and other entrepreneurial qualities. Because to grow globally, Japan lacks the linguistic skills, overengineers its products and fails to understand what might play well abroad. Nor is it an accident that Japanese researchers boast the most recipients of the Ig Nobel prizes, an annual satirical award presented by the “Annals of Improbable Research” science humor magazine.

“Japan’s puzzling foot-dragging on the tech illustrates an overlooked aspect of its innovation drive — its long history of brilliant innovations that were, for various reasons, overlooked and sidetracked.”

A New Kind Of Innovation

There was even a craze called Chindōgu for what became known as useless “curious or strange tools,” in the ‘80s and ‘90s when Japan actually made stuff the world wanted.

This Galápagosian inward focus, while fostering some unique innovations, has also left Japan isolated in the global tech landscape, or so the thinking goes. This created a superficially hi-tech Japan, Hideki Onda, a former Apple director, once told me.

Onda believed Japan’s deeply cautious and conservative business and political classes were the root cause. This allowed Japan to evolve along Galápagos lines because the ruthless nature of startup capitalism and radical technocratic disruption was such a poor fit for Japan’s slower, more considered way of doing things.

When economists were chivying for the re-ignition of Japan’s competitive “animal spirits,” the country responded with its trademark animal caution.

To best illustrate this, Onda recalled a time in 1996 when Apple was pushing Japan to introduce its teaching tech to schools. The education minister’s answer was a polite “Kekko desu,” or no.

Apple’s then-CEO Michael Spindler asked Onda when they might return to try again. “When the ‘60s-era floor indicator above the ministry’s elevator door goes digital,” Onda told him.

A decisively Luddite response, many thought at the time. But fast-forward through 30 years of digitization, and we are seeing method in the minister’s madness. The rush to digitization and the digital economy, we found belatedly, has resulted in its own casualties .

The American models of capital efficiency and market disruption we so admired are now being seen as possibly ruinous. We are learning, for one, that networked screen-based learning is no silver bullet. Nor do all cultures suit the startup models; just ask the equal-with-Japan on social-cohesion-first Swedes. Read Noema in print.

The Medium Is The Message

After noting a drop in student literacy, Sweden has now reversed its push toward digital learning. Cellphones have been banned in schools, and the textbook industry rejoices at schools’ return to paper.

And yet the assault from a proselytizing Big Tech on Japan, where digitization has been slow and AI remains largely a curiosity in the workplace, is intensifying.

There is still an unfulfilled desire to digitize; that is true. Broadcast mainly from some business quarters and certain politicos. Japan’s AI regulations, for instance, have been made as loose as those in the U.S., and many see them as an incentive for American corporations to move in.

I asked a Japanese friend and tech journalist what he thought about this new “Black Ships” moment, and he told me he expects an awkward culture clash of Titanic proportions. “Because American technology companies are often extraordinarily irresponsible about the social consequences of what they build.”

He had another keen observation for me: “Ultimately, Silicon Valley is not primarily optimized to maximize human wellbeing. It is optimized to maximize returns.”

Japan. Ostensibly capitalistic, has a rather different take. The emphasis is on social cohesion, not profits. This contrast is not simply cultural. In a 2006 Japanese government survey, nearly 70% of responding Japanese companies said employees were important stakeholders, and 90% planned to maintain long-term employment.

He now suspects that when we look back several decades, or perhaps several centuries, from now, we may conclude that our current tech revolution produces too much “technological pollution” — innovations that ultimately caused considerable suffering to large numbers of people despite Silicon Valley’s innovative bent. This is particularly daunting in light of well-informed concerns that AI development will lead to our extinction.

His conclusion echoes Japan’s nascent clarion call for “technological sovereignty.” It is now the responsibility, not of America, but of countries with long histories and deep cultural traditions such as in Europe, Japan and elsewhere, to propose ways of using technology that engage much more seriously with social responsibility, he argues.

And it is true that some Europeans and Japanese are now working to reduce their dependency on U.S. tech. But when you don’t have the cards, a certain raspy voice likes to remind us, the white flag your pushy competitors hand you can seem like a lifesaver after all.

Techno Darwinism Dawns

Until the triumph of such heretics, the inescapable dark logic of techno Darwinism gets to cast its shade far into Japan’s corridors of power for now. Supping with the Devil as a hedge against total irrelevance, you might want to call it. Just bring long chopsticks and hope you are not on the menu.

“The rush to digitization and the digital economy, we found belatedly, has resulted in its own casualties.”

Presiding over national decline and a plummeting yen, Peter Thiel’s recent appearance in Tokyo must have seemed an omen of sorts to the government — perhaps even an opportunity. Certainly, Japan’s premier Sanae Takaichi received Thiel and his trade mission cheerfully enough, despite any whiff of sulfur. Besides being something of a missionary from the darker side of the Singularity faithful, his visit was the latest in a long list of tech emissaries from across the water. U.S. venture capital, too, is arriving fast. Marc Andreessen , boss of one of the heftiest firms, opened his first overseas office in Japan this summer. It is no secret that Japan now sees the Silicon Valley model as the one that might get it out of its considerable hole.

Brandon Hill, founder of an outfit that helps startups on both sides of the Pacific, told me Tokyo is desperate for more startups and more “successful exits.” The hope is that those eager entrepreneurs will spark another period of rapid reinvention like the 19th-century’s Meiji-era modernization, or Japan’s dramatic re-industrialization after World War II. This one, we imagine, will be driven by homegrown Silicon-Valley wannabes with less perishable wings of wax.

But Japan should be thinking beyond simply creating more startups, Hill insists, keen to impart to an attentive Japan the magic formula: “It should be creating more globally competitive companies.”

Death March, What Death March?

But these are death march orders again. Because given Japan’s current climate of anxiety and its lack of survival skills, English and narrative nous, the global market will exact its toll. Once a nation of outward-looking, inveterate tinkerers willing to make technology central to national survival, the collapse of the ‘80s economic boom in 1991 led to lost decades and economic stagnation. The bust also created a fear of risk-taking and a retreat into safe jobs, safe investments and safe conservative governments.

Thanks to that trauma, contemporary Japan is a much more inward-looking and risk-averse place now. The bubble’s collapse and the financial crisis that followed gave way to a long corporate decline. In a 2024 survey , the Bank of Japan found that many firms had curbed investment and built cash reserves after the crisis and later shocks. That history helps explain business caution, though it cannot by itself explain Japan’s wider inward turn.

The moral and institutional habits formed by Japan’s lost decades are unlikely to evaporate at the urging of a few Tech Valley gurus. Many here, perhaps rightly, take pride that the Libertarian, go-getting style of the buccaneering new world capitalists remains as rare as buttered sushi.

Despite this, some sections of central government, such as the bullish Ministry of Economy, are insisting the nation pledges its shirt to such a miraculous resurrection of entrepreneurial spirits. Even if it means the much-dreaded importing — however imperfectly — of alien business practices, plus accommodating the Devil of foreign investment and all its stratagems.

The current thinking is, if Japan’s satraps are to become Satan’s latest freshly minted imps so that the country can flourish, so be it. Accordingly, Japan’s ministries must undergo a Damascene conversion, buckle under for universal digitization, get with the program and ditch the fax for the splendid shining lie of the startup. Strong medicine for a nation that swears by “not waking the baby.”

The Revolution Will Not Be Commodified

As already mentioned, the revolution will not be restricted to business. Shanghaied into the program are its universities, too, to be raided for startup recruits. They now giddily employ the magic word salads of “incubators,” “ecosystems” and “unicorns” — incantations in the newly imported, and hopefully profitable, cargo cult.

In service to the “Stack” — the secret sauce of the vaunted digital product — they must dump the Old-Fogey seats of learning/babysitting roles and learn to “hyper-scale.” And in doing so, become the engines of a “new technology-driven nation” where science and technology provide economic growth and national security. The model is California’s lucrative fusion of pioneering lab work and entrepreneurship stripped for export.

This is a big ask for an institution whose principal role, until now, was an untaxing refuge for students lately overtaxed by Japan’s notorious entrance exams.

But the heart wants what the heart wants. So out must go the playground-cum-finishing school model applied to the young before they join the workforce. It is a system that makes them easy targets for job automation anyway.

“The moral and institutional habits formed by Japan’s lost decades are unlikely to evaporate at the urging of a few Tech Valley gurus.”

Research at the top universities is another matter entirely. World-class and innovative but sheltered from the worldly West Coast-style monetizing of know-how, they are an unlikely vehicle for commerce. But to the trendier, more tech-savvy of Tokyo’s mandarins, gifting academic researchers with money and startup blueprints must seem like a foolproof remedy for Japan’s economic woes.

The country’s economic emergency is real enough. Japan’s nominal GDP, which once ranked second in the world, fell to third place in 2010 and then to fourth place in 2023. The country’s share of global nominal GDP has fallen sharply, from approximately 18% in 1995 to approximately 3.8% in 2025. More worryingly, its nominal GDP per capita has also fallen from second in the world to 38th today.

Real wages have stagnated for 30 years; the yen has fallen to a low not seen for nearly 40 years.

Ingredients But No Recipe

But there are reasons for hope. After all, the country has all the ingredients to make it a supreme techno-state. Elite scientists, a magic-money spigot (take a bow, quantitative easing and near-zero interest rates) and world-class manufacturing chops.

But instead of impacting our world with its surprisingly useful research applications, the policies, as my tech writer friend pointed out, are only exposing an almighty clash of civilizations. It’s another institutional mismatch where Japanese universities, slow and hierarchical to their bones, repurpose poorly as startup factory incubators (which must be fast and unstable). The friction is almost palpable.

After decades of being left to their own insular devices — including, bizarrely, a reluctance to publish abroad — university-linked founders are now lining up to take grants for “global startups” while conveniently skipping the global part. No slogan has ever been emptier than “be global from the start,” as most of these founders don’t speak English .

But without the “ go global !” declaration, they would be unlikely to qualify for funding. This makes Japan’s latest bid to race across borders, like all its other vaunted internationalization schemes, a sham.

Because Japan lingers in the bottom ranks of English proficiency tests and belatedly adopts international marketing practices, like pitching or self-promotion, its innovation remains mostly invisible to a broader public.

Without a sudden sea-change, conjuring national self-reliance, economic security and cutting-edge innovation out of Japan’s unbelievably stuffy, risk-averse and archaic institutions will be a miracle. Already, in critical fields like AI, semiconductors and defense tech, the chance to lead sailed away with the last of the country’s frustrated emigre innovators.

Enter The Zombies

But appealing fictions have a habit of overriding the stark facts. So universities take a substantial amount of government money to pump out startups despite being poorly equipped to produce global-ready startups as the state is requesting. Most of these universities focus on Japan’s stockpile of zombie enterprises — the kinds that have stayed alive thanks to cheap credit and government handouts rather than healthy, global market performance.

Japanese startups outside the blessed and coddled circle of academia fare no better. Lacking the swagger of Silicon Valley, Japan’s corporate culture is the antithesis of America’s individualistic, T-shirted tycoons. Japan’s corporate culture prioritizes conformist don’t-rock-the-boat mediocrity, uses generalists rather than specialists, and favors risk-aversion over disruptive ideas; monetizing innovation will remain a struggle. The Economist suggests Tokyo’s “startups first” growth plan looks woefully misguided.

Not that the country lacks the kind of Promethean chutzpah that could bring new light, energy and progress. But Japan has a habit of taking the role of an angry Zeus — chaining any unruly innovators to the nearest rock. Japan has a long list of disgruntled innovators who feel hard done by its corporate system. Even the chap who invented the white LED, Shuji Nakamura , was originally rewarded with a corporate bonus of just 20,000 yen (roughly $200 at the time).

Scapegoat

If there is one man famous for bringing raw, individualistic U.S.-style techno-capitalism to these shores and failing spectacularly, it is Takefumi Horie — AKA “Horiemon.” No fire-bearing Titan to mankind is he — more an ambitious internet provider — but instructive all the same was the treatment of this tech startup founder imprisoned for 21 months for his disruptive antics a couple of decades ago.

Horie’s style put him at the center of a culture clash between U.S. and Japanese business. He became the scourge of Japanese companies when his internet firm Livedoor launched a hostile bid for Nippon Broadcasting in 2005. Using a legal loophole in off-hours trading, it bought 29.6% of the radio broadcaster in one go, bringing its holding to around a third. It was an attempt to take control of the powerful Fuji TV. The move led the government to change the Securities and Exchange law to extend takeover rules to off-hours trading. The bid failed.

“Japan’s corporate culture prioritizes conformist don’t-rock-the-boat mediocrity, uses generalists rather than specialists, and favors risk-aversion over disruptive ideas; monetizing innovation will remain a struggle.”

Authorities arrested Horie a year later on a separate issue. He faced charges that his company Livedoor falsified financial results to mislead investors. The company reported a pretax profit of about 5 billion yen, but prosecutors said it had actually made a loss of about 300 million yen. Horie was convicted of securities-law violations and sentenced to 2 ½ years in prison, serving about 21 months.

Such treatment shocked Japan’s startup community and signaled that non-consensus-driven, Anglo-Saxon, morally ambiguous capitalism bent on erasing cultural norms might be tolerated in the U.S. but punished in Japan. Japanese tech startups aiming to be the tallest poppy at the time quickly pulled up their roots. The startup revolution and rush to digitization were canceled.

In the face of Japan’s bureaucratic top-down planning, Japan’s elite universities, patient capital and strong manufacturing record count for little. Fast-moving, software-driven global tech trends simply move on — too quickly for a Japanese catch-up.

This, despite Japan actually sharing the passion for tech America does. In the field of AI in particular, Japan’s affair with machine intelligence is relatively long and productive. Computer scientist Noriko Arai sat me down in her office 15 years ago and explained how a “mad scientist” dream of humanoid robots placed Japan ahead in the AI race decades ago.

In the 1980s, while Western researchers were still skeptical of neural networks, Japanese scientists were diving deep into artificial neurons and machine learning. “We say Japan was ahead at the time,” AI researcher Yutaka Matsuo told me. “But perhaps that doesn’t mean a lot now.”

Japan fell behind, failing to catch the St. Vitus’s dance deemed necessary to animate a Silicon Valley-style digital resurrection. But perhaps we have been measuring the wrong thing. Yes, its institutions are often too conservative to change, but as we survey the damage that technology has inflicted upon us, were the plodders right to plod?

Fearlessness in the face of failure, rapid iteration, global self-confidence, impatience with hierarchy — are definitively not the country’s house style. But because of this, did Japan eventually dodge a bullet? My tech journalist friend and others like him increasingly feel so.

There are fears of a too-rapidly deployed foreign AI risk, fears over the erosion of social cohesion, fears that a gig economy will replace Japan’s cherished full employment. The call is also for more strategic autonomy from tech corporations who are outmaneuvering the locals.

Black Ships Redux

But the chatter is not just of another Black Ships “coup” or “digital colonialism” if Japan adopts the American model of rapid disruption. There’s a growing realization that the friction of the culture clash is perhaps a benefit. Japan’s plodding ways and institutions incompatible with hyper-capitalism offer a chance to install some kind of rugged technological sovereignty. They allow Japan to escape the technological determinism now infecting the West.

The appearance of a technology doesn’t mean that societies are suddenly forced to adapt to it. Societies should decide which technologies to adopt, how quickly, under what rules and for whose benefit. In 2021, UNESCO called for human oversight and demanded that we give societies a basis to accept or reject AI systems. A call now responded to belatedly by institutions and governments worldwide, mirroring people’s concerns over AI developments.

Coincidentally, Johnson’s ill-timed Fintech speech I attended at the embassy shines a light on the assumption that every problem has a technological solution, and that more technology necessarily means progress. A technological determinism and the myth of technological progressiveness Japan should be keen to avoid.

“We have to recognize that disruptive technology is simply inevitable and we cannot put the technological genie back in the bottle,” Johnson added to his contactless payments pitch. “Once the toothpaste is out of the tube, folks, that’s it.”

Inertia Is Not All Bad News

Do the Japanese need to become more Californian to be more capable, or should these old institutions and Japan’s inertia be left alone to create some breathing space? Bill Gates said recently there is “no plan to ease the entry into the AI era.” Perhaps Japan’s experience of friction at that very entry is telling us something. Despite its half-hearted attempts to mimic Silicon Valley values, the country’s deep inertia seems to be buffeting it from some of the ill effects of globalization and technological disruption.

For decades, Japanese companies have attempted to shield their workers from the insatiable demands of stockholders and capital as part of a “social responsibility” mindset to help create jobs and safeguard companies.

“As outdated and sluggish as the nation’s institutions might be, their limbic caution has preserved livelihoods.”

As outdated and sluggish as the nation’s institutions might be, their limbic caution has preserved livelihoods. Because, as it has often been said, Japan is a massive job creation scheme. Any introduction of American-style lean capitalism would threaten the labor policies aimed at creating overemployment, and the men I see guiding traffic around roadworks outside my house where a traffic light would do would all be out of a job. Making Japan a possible, and unlikely, last stand to our current reckoning with technological determinism.

Everywhere else the old rules are breaking, and some are heading for the exit laden with unicorn silver. West Coast billionaires are even reportedly seeking escape hatches or bunkers. Could tardy Japan be on their list of hideaways?

Exchange Tokyo for Vienna in this old joke and you’ll see what I mean. “If the world should ever come to an end — move to Vienna, because everything there happens 20 years later,” goes the quip used even today about the celestial city.

Japan is not unlike Vienna in this respect in its refusal to update. And its failure to do so, like the unabashed, unreconstructed British Embassy in Tokyo, may not be a disadvantage at all. On the contrary, it can remind us of what we value, and why.

stories.title: The Sediment Of Culture Shapes Political Order

stories.body:
Governing systems are effective when power, ideology and deep culture are aligned.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

As a global journal of ideas, Noema receives feedback from readers all over the world that broadens our way of seeing and kindles the further iteration of our thinking. One recent case is a response by Carl Gay, an executive of the Cloudspago consultancy in Australia, to the Noema essay “When The Present Eats The Future: The Achilles Heel of Consumer Democracies.”

In that essay, I contrast post-Mao China’s capacity for reaching a consensus on long-term goals and determinedly implementing them over many years without a break in continuity with the increasing inability of consumer democracies to do so. The example I used in the context of climate change was how China set the goal decades ago of dominating green technology, especially electric vehicles and batteries, and has steadily achieved that objective, while most open societies of the West have sputtered behind. Its “whole dragon” approach brings the resources of the entire system to bear on the challenge at hand.

I pointed out that the strength of China’s system is closely related to its chief flaw: enforcing order and repressing freedom to keep the consensus from fraying. In his note to Noema, Gay makes explicit what I only implied: To the extent China’s determined continuity clogs corrective feedback loops, a policy ordained by the Party can go off in the wrong direction for a very long time, causing damage not easily repaired.

The example he uses is the disastrous one-child policy that held from 1980-2015. It resulted in today’s demographic implosion, where there are not enough young people to sustain the welfare of an aging society. Indeed, blinkered assumptions from the present, projected forward, robbed the future of a balanced population.

Another less calamitous case in point was the 2022 COVID lockdown, which went on well past the patience of a restless public. In that case, the nascent feedback loops of contagious online rants, instances of journalistic exposure and even episodic outbursts of public demonstration resulted in a responsive and more immediate change in policy.

“Deep culture always returns to shape a society in a way similar to how a person’s emotional subconscious is forever biting at the heels of rational cognition.”

The Equivalent Of Market Signals In Politics

The big question for China’s one-party juggernaut is whether it can accommodate corrective feedback mechanisms in politics that are equivalent to the market signals it accommodates to check state-backed economic policy from going too far down the wrong path.

Two developments are emerging that impact this feedback deficit. Paradoxically, the first is that expanded surveillance from the top serves at the same time to register people’s dissatisfaction to the Party guardians listening at scale.

The other is that China’s densely wired society has become a ready platform for surveillance of official behavior from below, or sousveillance . Citizen reports, especially about corruption, rapidly gain virality when posted online.

This dual potential is not lost on the authorities. In a candid conversation in Beijing in 2015, China’s then cyber czar, Lu Wei, openly acknowledged that, in the absence of electoral accountability, an active netizenry can be a critical channel for sending rectifying signals from the grassroots to the Party hierarchy. Even the choice of keyword searches used to invoke censorship can be considered a form of feedback.

Needless to say, if the receiver is not attuned to the signal frequency, the message will go unheard. Read Noema in print.

Beyond that, a Shanghai entrepreneur I know who was a founder of YouKu, China’s version of YouTube, has told me how the Party is constantly polling down to the neighborhood level to gauge any discontent that may be bubbling up.

China scholar John Keane goes so far as to suggest that China is becoming a kind of “phantom democracy.” By that, he means “the fear of democracy forces a style of political management that in many ways mirrors and mimics electoral systems, where the fear of elections puts leaders in a constant campaign mode” as they feel the need to continually convince constituencies of their worthiness and legitimacy.

But Gay’s key insight in his reply to the Noema essay is more profound and is a larger frame for understanding why China functions as well as it does in contrast to consumer democracies.

“Culture is the substructure upon which the superstructure of ideology, politics and economics are built — the opposite of how modern thought would have it.”

Accumulated Culture Matters Most

As Gay puts it, “power, ideology and culture run at three speeds. Power changes in years, ideology in decades, culture in generations. China’s ‘whole dragon’ approach works because all three are aligned: a power layer that sets fifty-year goals, an ideology that makes its accountability internal and a culture with two thousand years of examination-system deference deposited in it. The continuity you admire is what alignment produces.

“Consumer democracies have the opposite shape: a return channel for error and no continuity. But ‘a governing consensus that sticks’ is a power-layer prescription, and consensus can’t be installed at the power layer when the culture isn’t carrying it. The rules change; the people don’t. Democracies lack a constituency for the future not because opinion is fickle but because the culture hasn’t yet accumulated the consequences that would create one. It will, when the damage becomes undeniable. That is slower than the climate clock allows, but it’s the only route the mechanism offers.”

Gay expanded on this useful frame elsewhere in an essay titled, “Power, Ideology And Culture: The Sediment Beneath Politics.”

“Political order is not one thing but three, moving at three different speeds,” Gay explains in his essay. “There is power — the hard architecture of institutions, coercion, money and command, the layer that can change in a season. There is ideology — the story a society tells about why those with power deserve it and why the rest should comply. And there is culture — the slow accumulation of everything a people has lived through, settled so deep that it is no longer argued but simply assumed. Most of our political commentary treats these as rival explanations: the institutionalist sees only power, the theorist only ideology, the culture critic only identity. Each is holding one limb of the animal.

“The reframe I would urge is this. Culture is not a third thing standing beside the other two. It is mostly the other two — power and ideology accumulated over generations and set hard, the way sediment is only the silt from yesteryear’s flood waters deposited over time, slowly compressing to a firmer sedimentary structure. What a people will accept, resist or demand today is the settled residue of the power arrangements and the justifying stories it absorbed long before anyone now living was old enough to question them. This is why culture is the slowest layer to move, and why, when it finally does move, power and ideology have no choice but to follow.”

Deep culture always returns to shape a society in a way similar to how a person’s emotional subconscious is forever biting at the heels of rational cognition. Culture is the substructure upon which the superstructure of ideology, politics and economics are built — the opposite of how modern thought would have it.

As political orders around the world enter a protracted period of upheaval, Gay’s frame of whether they are aligned or not with their cultural grounding is one of the more compelling paradigms for making sense of it all.

Decision by MPC a week after the budget comes as Iran war continues to drive up energy costs

Business live – latest updates

The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to come, to combat soaring inflation unleashed by the Iran war.

Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the move, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase.

The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices persistently above $100 in recent months, as hopes evaporated of a deal that could reopen the key strait of Hormuz .

As a result, the Bank now expects UK inflation to spike to 4.9% in the middle of next year – up from 3.2% in its last economic forecast, in July. Inflation hit 3.5% in September , as measured on the consumer prices index.

The decision, which will hit mortgage borrowers, comes a week after John Healey used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers. Echoing the Office of Budget Responsibility’s gloomy forecasts for living standards , the MPC expects real post-tax income to fall, this year and next.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, raised the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

“Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach,” he said, in the MPC minutes.

However, he played down the likelihood of a prolonged series of increases, as markets have been predicting. “Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence in hikes. But, unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase,” he said. The Bank’s next interest rate decision will be announced on 17 December.

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, in the wake of Democrat victories in the US Congress, which some investors interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, blamed the war, and its impact on inflation, for the rout.

Explaining their decision to raise borrowing costs, the MPC highlighted the pass-through from elevated oil prices to business and consumer costs across the economy. It expects the Ofgem energy cap, which determines household bills, to rise to £2,150 in January; and to increase again in April. Food price inflation could hit 4.75% by mid-2027, it warns.

Businesses have so far reported in the Bank’s surveys that they have been able to absorb soaring oil and gas prices – by hedging their energy costs, for example – but the MPC believes they will soon have to start passing them on to consumers, in higher prices.

after newsletter promotion

They are also concerned about workers seeking to offset the impact of the higher cost of living, by bidding for bumper pay rises.

While the decision to hike rates was supported by all MPC members, the minutes of the meeting reveal stark divisions over how much further they may need to go, to bring inflation under control. The dovish Alan Taylor suggested this should be a “risk-management “one-for-now” insurance hike”, while Mann argued that an immediate half-point rise was necessary, to restore the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility.

Healey’s budget included measures aimed at cushioning the impact of higher energy prices – including extending the fuel duty freeze, and the VAT cut on electricity bills. The MPC said the package would shave a quarter percentage point off inflation in mid-2027.

Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”

It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.

MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.

The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025 , a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.

Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.

However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.

after newsletter promotion

The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.

The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.

“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.

As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.

“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.

A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

stories.body:
Bank of England decision

Newsflash: The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years, as policymakers try to fight rising inflation.

Its monetary policy committee has voted to raise Bank rate from 3.75% to 4%, the first rise since August 2023.

The move was widely expected by markets, as UK inflation recently hit 3.5% , further above the Bank’s 2% target.

Excitingly, one member – Catherine Mann – wanted a half-point hike!

The Bank says:

double quotation mark At its meeting ending on 4 November 2026, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted by a majority of 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%. One member voted to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%.

How the MPC was split 8-1

Today’s interest rate decision was taken by the nine members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee.

Eight of them – Andrew Bailey , Sarah Breeden , Swati Dhingra , Megan Greene , Clare Lombardelli , Huw Pill , Dave Ramsden and Alan Taylor – voted for the quarter-point rise.

The Bank says:

double quotation mark The duration and scale of the energy price increase had generated sufficient inflationary pressures in the pipeline to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. There was a range of views among these members about the extent to which the underlying disinflationary process prior to the conflict had continued, the degree of spare capacity in the economy, and the restrictiveness of the current monetary policy stance. These members agreed that, although evidence of second-round effects had been limited, the availability of evidence would increase over time, and would continue to need close monitoring, along with the implications of developments in energy prices for medium-term inflationary risks.

The outlier was Catherine L Mann, who voted for a half-point rise in Bank rate.

Mann is concerned about the “non-linear inflation risks” facing the UK, and keen to stamp on higher wage demands.

She explains, in the minutes of the meeting,

double quotation mark Households are particularly attentive to energy and food price inflation, which may be reflected in 2027 wage demands. With CPI inflation at 3.5% in September, the economy has crossed the estimated statistical threshold into a high inflation-tight labour market regime where the asymmetric behavioural responses of households and firms support more robust second-round effects. A different research approach estimates that the economy may well have breached the policy credibility threshold, which worsens the policy trade-off. Moreover, a substantial inflation risk premium is in the UK yield curve, reflecting five years of above-target inflation, where it has averaged 4.7%. Therefore, from a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is ‘good policy’.

Bank: Inflation to rise to around 5% by next summer

The Bank of England is also warning that UK inflation is set to hit 5% by the middle of next year, as it explains why it raised interest rates today.

That would be a serious, painful acceleration in prices – inflation was clocked at 3.5% in September – hurting households who are already struggling under the cost of living crisis.

The Bank pins the blame on the Iran war saying:

double quotation mark The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month. Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level. UK CPI inflation increased to 3.5% in September. It is now expected to rise to around 5% by the middle of next year. It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation.

The Bank says:

double quotation mark At its meeting ending on 4 November 2026, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted by a majority of 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%. One member voted to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%.

BoE rate hike probability over 99%

Excitement is building, as the City prepares for the Bank of England’s latest interest decision to be announced at noon sharp.

A rate hike is nailed on, according to the money markets – they show that a quarter-point rise to 4%, from 3.75%, is a 99.96% chance.

That part of the decision, therefore, probably won’t be the important part of the story.

George Vessey at cross-border payments company Convera, explains:

double quotation mark With markets assigning around a 95% probability to such an outcome, attention instead turns to the vote split, updated forecasts and Governor Bailey’s guidance. Markets currently price almost 100bp of additional tightening through late 2027, a path that looks increasingly ambitious in our view. If the BoE pushes back against those expectations, the resulting dovish repricing in rates could prove more important for sterling than the hike itself.

FTSE 250 hits alltime high

Britain’s share index of medium-sized companies has hit a record high today.

The FTSE 250 index, which includes companies who are too small for the FTSE 100, has hit a new peak – it was up 1% or 261 points to a high of 25,176 points.

AstraZeneca "made $10bn offer for Rhythm pharmaceuticals"

In the pharmaceutical world, AstraZeneca has reportedly made a $10bn offer to buy US biotech firm Rhythm.

According to the Wall Street Journal , AstraZeneca made an offer last month – a deal would allow it to expand its portfolio of rare disease treatments, as Rhythm ​develops therapies for rare neuroendocrine disorders.

Shares in Rhythm jumped yesterday afternoon after the WSJ said AstraZeneca had offered to pay $124 a share. This pushed Rhythm’s shares up by 28% to $110.68. They’re slightly lower (-3%) in pre-market trading.

AstraZeneca has declined to comment.

The pound is “enjoying a significant resurgence” as the UK’s reputation for stability returns, argues Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

double quotation mark Slightly stronger-than-expected growth, expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates today, and signs of a rapprochement with Europe are all helping to bolster the currency. There is a sense that the UK is beginning to be viewed in a more favourable light by international investors, with its reputation for stability starting to regain some lustre. Political and economic difficulties across the Channel, particularly in France, are also providing a stark contrast. And the improving relationship with Europe could offer a further boost to growth further down the line, if it translates into fewer trade frictions and closer economic cooperation.

Why Trump’s midterms defeat has pushed down energy prices

Oil markets sold off aggressively because the political power shift within the US could lead to “more scrutiny over the war, while funding it could become more difficult”, according to market analysts at Dutch bank ING.

“How all this plays out is still highly uncertain,” ING’s analysts added. “Therefore, the degree and speed to which the oil market has sold off seems to be overdone.”

Professor Brenda Shaffer , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council Global Energy Center , told the Guardian that although the Democrats won support by galvanising the public opposition to rising energy costs they would struggle to address the crisis that helped the party to victory.

Shaffer said:

double quotation mark “They may blame the Republicans for the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and continue to do so, but why would Iran compromise now?”

She added that the record high diesel prices in the US which have pushed up costs across the economy may also prove difficult to tackle if Democrats are unwilling to curtail Ukraine’s military attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia, one of the world’s biggest diesel exporters.

Gas and oil prices fall after midterms

Donald Trump’s mid-term election defeat has caused Europe’s gas prices to tumble as global energy markets bet on a quicker than expected resolution to the strait of Hormuz crisis.

The market price for oil, gas and fuels across global markets plummeted after the US President conceded that the US-Israeli war on Iran had angered voters and caused his part to lose control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The admission triggered oil and gas prices to fall sharply as the election results emerged on the hope that the result may galvanise US efforts to end the conflict, which has disrupted energy supplies through the strait of Hormuz for over 8 months.

Europe’s gas benchmark fell to three week lows of €84.36 per megawatt hour on Thursday after climbing to a four year high of almost €104 per megawatt hour late last week as colder weather prompted companies to begin drawing from Europe’s historically low gas storage facilities .

Europe’s gas stores are only around 74% full, well below the five-year seasonal average of 90%. In Germany, Europe’s biggest economy and home to the EU’s largest gas stores, gas reserves stand at below 61%.

The gas market slump followed a sharp drop in the global oil benchmark, Brent crude, which fell 8.7% lower on Wednesday to below $95 a barrel, its lowest price in two months.

The pound might strengthen today, depending on what the Bank of England says at lunchtime.

With a rate hike widely expected, the City will be more interested in how united Bank policymakers are on the decision, and what guidance the BoE gives about future rate hikes.

Charalampos Pissouros , senior market analyst at Trading Point , explains:

double quotation mark As for the pound, traders are keeping their gaze locked on the Bank of England decision today. With UK inflation accelerating to 3.5% year-on-year in September, investors are nearly certain that policymakers will raise rates for the first time since August 2023. Therefore, the pound is unlikely to be driven by the hike itself, but by the vote, the updated economic projections and the guidance on further tightening. A unanimous vote for an increase, upwardly revised inflation projections and strong willingness to continue with more rate increases could add fuel to sterling’s engines.

Pound hits highest level since Brexit vote

Newsflash: The pound has hit its highest level since its crash after the Brexit referendum a decade ago.

Data released by the Bank of England shows that the pound reached its strongest level against a basket of other currencies since 23 June 2016 – the day of the EU vote - yesterday.

This follows the drop in the value of the US dollar after the Midterm elections, but also reflects the pound’s recent strength against other currencies such as the euro and the yen.

The pound has also benefited from expectations that the BoE will raise interest rates at noon today, which makes it more lucrative for investors to hold funds in sterling.

The dollar weakened generally yesterday, amid a risk-on rally that saw money flow into other currencies.

Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank explains:

double quotation mark When it came to the market reaction, there was relief among investors that the results weren’t disputed, which helped to reduce political uncertainty. Moreover, the prospect of divided government also eased concerns about the fiscal trajectory, given it’ll now be more difficult to pass tax cuts or spending packages.

Today’s 10-year high relates to the sterling “effective exchange rate index” ( EERI ), which tracks the pound against a basket of other currencies.

Calculated by the Bank of England, this index has now hit 86.5372.

On the index, 100 equals the value of the pound in January 2005.

Back in 2016, the pound hit a 31-year low against the dollar . That pulled the EERI down to 84.441 on 24 June 2026, down from 87.9248 on the day of the referendum.

The EERI fell as low as 73.1 on March 23, 2020, in the Covid pandemic.

UK housebuilding slumps

Ouch! Activity in the UK’s construction sector fell sharply last month, new data shows.

The latest Constrution PMI report, just relased, shows there was a “sharp and accelerated reduction in business activity during October”.

Housebuilding work slumped in the month, the report says:

double quotation mark Residential activity (index at 35.1) was by far the weakest performing segment, with the latest reading the lowest since December 2025 and indicative of a steep drop in house building. Anecdotal evidence cited low consumer confidence, elevated risk aversion and headwinds from rising borrowing costs.

The overall Construction PMI , produced by S&P Global, has dropped to 43.6, down from 46.1 in September. That’s the lowest reading since June, and further below the 50-point mark showing stagnation.

One question pondered by investors and economists is how high UK interest rates might go.

Professor Costas Milas , of the Management School at the University of Liverpool , has published new forecasts for Bank Rate, in a blog post for the LSE Business Review .

He reports:

A Bank Rate of 4% (almost certainly today) is just outside the upper bound of neutral rates; so, policy is “borderline” restrictive. That said, I am critical of the whole concept of neutral rates and agree with [Fed chair] Kevin Warsh*.

The models I use suggest that Bank Rate will peak at 4.25% in mid 2027. We could see Bank Rate close to 4.6% in mid-2027 if, and only if, the BoE thought (unlikely at the moment) that inflation would stay as high as 4.2% up until 2028Q1.

[ * – Warsh recently said the neutral rate is “useful academically” but has no “operational effect” on policy decisions ]

Norway leaves interest rates on hold

Norway’s central bank has left interest rates on hold, but warned it could raise borrowing costs in the months ahead.

Norges Bank voted to maintain its policy rate at 4.5%, despite inflation continuing to run over its target.

Governor Ida Wolden Bache says:

double quotation mark “Inflation is too high. It will likely be necessary to keep the policy rate elevated for a time, and we are prepared to raise the policy rate if needed to bring inflation down to target within a reasonable time horizon.”

Isio: Markets welcome US midterm results, but key risks remain

While financial markets are welcoming the US midterm results, there are still some key risks, cautions Ajith Nair, chief investment officer of Isio Investment Management.

Nair explains that the reduced political uncertainty is helpful for markets – but that doesn’t mean that all the major risks have disappeared":

double quotation mark “The immediate reaction has clearly been positive and provides some welcome respite after the recent wobble in AI-related stocks. Markets appear to be taking comfort from the idea that the election result means the Trump administration will face greater constraints in pursuing some of the more disruptive parts of its policy agenda over the final two years of the presidency. “That may ultimately prove correct, but investors should be careful about getting too comfortable with that assumption. A more challenging Congress does not mean the President is powerless, particularly when it comes to trade and foreign policy. If markets are effectively betting on two relatively uneventful years from Washington, that assumption could still be tested.”

US midterm elections – live updates

After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?

US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the midterm elections , lifted by hopes that Donald Trump ’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.

The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party won control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The price of oil dropped sharply as traders assessed the impact of the Democrats’ win on the war in Iran. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell below $100 a barrel for the first time since early October.

In a social media post on Wednesday afternoon, Trump took credit for the jump. “Stock Market just hit another Record High,” he wrote. “Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!”

However, the US dollar fell against the currencies of America’s major trading partners, hitting a one-month low on Wednesday while coming under pressure from falling bond yields. Investors moved into US treasuries, viewed as a haven from the political gridlock anticipated during the rest of Trump’s final term in office.

The dollar index, which measures it against a basket of six currencies, slid to its lowest level in a month, with the pound hitting its highest level since mid-September on the back of a fragile dollar, while the euro also made gains.

The dollar also slid against the yen and the Swiss franc, currencies that traders tend to turn to during times of uncertainty.

Meanwhile, the yield, or interest rate, on the benchmark 10-year US treasury bond has fallen 4.7 basis points to 4.918%. On two-year bonds it has dropped 3.7bps to 4.597%. Yields fall when bond prices rise.

Across the US, voters rejected Trump and the Republican agenda, with the Democrats securing Senate seats in traditional Republican strongholds such as Texas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina.

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the trading platform IG, said: “The scale of the losses will inevitably raise questions about Trump’s ability to push through his agenda over the next two years, and markets are already reacting. The dollar is under pressure as investors reassess the political outlook, while gold and silver are benefiting as safe haven plays.”

Futures trading initially indicated US stock markets would open sharply lower, with the Nasdaq expected to slide on fears over the prospects for AI companies. However, indicators later suggested Wall Street could open higher as Trump’s conciliatory tone and rises on European markets cheered investors.

European markets rose yesterday. London’s FTSE 100 was up 1.8%, Germany’s Dax rose by 2.2%, France’s Cac 40 was 2% higher and Italy’s FTSE MiB index rose by 2.2%.

Bank and clean energy stocks, which have borne the brunt of Trump’s policies, were among the top risers in Europe. Bank stocks rose by 2.8%, while Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems jumped nearly 5% and Ørsted soared 7.4%.

“Some individual names are nursing significant losses today,” said Kathleen Brooks, the UK research director at XTB. “SpaceX is down 5% in the premarket, and Tesla is lower by more than 4%. Elon Musk is considered an anathema to most Democrats.”

Musk, the world’s richest person, pumped $446m (£331m) into the midterms, funding Republican-aligned political action committees and groups.

after newsletter promotion

Brooks said investors were reacting to expectations that a Democrat-controlled Congress could mean greater scrutiny for AI companies, which could also cast doubt on a potential merger of Musk’s two companies.

The price of gold, a traditional haven asset, rose by 2.2%, soaring past $4,000 an ounce.

AI-related shares tumbled during Asian trading hours, on expectations that Democrats will want to bring in greater regulation of the sector.

Chris Turner, the global head of markets at ING, said: “Investors will be parsing what this all means. For example, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race on a ticket of wanting an immediate moratorium on datacentre buildouts.”

He added: “Given AI’s role in powering the US economy , speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capital expenditure plans briefly hit markets.”

Jesper Koll, an expert director at the financial services company Monex Group, said: “The AI momentum has turned negative, with or without the Republicans having a majority. The starting point for financial markets into this election, particularly for the equity market, has been adverse on AI.”

Trump’s style of governing through executive orders has prompted some analysts to question whether the Democrats regaining control of Congress will have much change on US policymaking.

“There’s still a number of areas where Donald Trump can influence the markets – trade and tariffs, foreign policy and existing regulations,” said Tai Hui, a market strategist at JP Morgan Asset Management.

stories.body:
John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff

W ith four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic.

The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points.

They had been punished as part of a “special campaign to crack down on match-fixing, gambling and corruption in the football industry”, said a joint statement from the Chinese Football Association, the Ministry of Public Security and the General Administration of Sport at the time.

Chengdu were one of the seven to start on zero, above the defending champions Shanghai Port, who lost five points, and the runners-up Shanghai Shenhua who were hit with 10. It robbed the usual favourites of energy and it was all a bit surreal.

It almost felt over as soon as it started with Chengdu opening up a big lead, dropping just two points from the first 12 games while the usual powers struggled to get going.

Chengdu is a major city known more for its fiery Sichuan cuisine, genteel temples and cute pandas than football, despite English attempts to change that. In 2006, Sheffield United bought a local club but the Chengdu Blades were eventually dissolved in 2015. Four years later, City Football Group bought a stake in Sichuan Jiuniu but then moved the club to the southern city of Shenzhen in 2024.

Chengdu Rongcheng were formed in 2018, coming up through the divisions to finally, this season, be within touching distance of the championship. But just two wins from the past 13 and three defeats in a row mean the leaders are not limping to the line but have collapsed right next to it.

It should have been over weeks ago. On 10 October, more than 40,000 fans were ready to celebrate the title but an added‑time goal from Alberto Quiles gave Tianjin Jinmen Tiger a 1-0 win and postponed the celebrations. Next up was a trip to Shanghai Port but that ended in a 3-0 defeat. The penultimate game of the season came against challengers Dalian Yingbo, when again, just avoiding defeat was needed. It was another painful experience as they lost 1-0 after missing a first-half penalty and having a 90th-minute equaliser ruled out by the video assistant referee.

Chengdu have not scored in almost seven hours of football while Dalian are the form team with four consecutive wins. If they win a fifth against Tianjin then Chengdu need a point at fourth‑placed Shandong Taishan as the league is decided by head-to-head results before goal difference. Not many think they will. Even fewer hope so. Dalian and the 60,000 fans who attend home games are the people’s choice. Chengdu are not popular because their fans have developed a poor reputation. Last November, the club were fined about $70,000 (£52,200) after some home supporters racially abused Henan FC’s Ghanaian striker Frank Acheampong, just weeks after a punishment of $3,000 after travelling supporters at a Champions League game in South Korea threw bottles at the Ulsan HD players.

Whatever happens it is an unexpected and dramatic ending to a season that started in shock and the usual negative international headlines that surround Chinese football. The grandstand finish is welcome and average attendances have risen. They are poised to finish at about 30,000, a considerable jump from 25,755 last season and, by some distance, the best in Asia. Regional leagues have been enjoying some popularity too, showing that there is genuine love for the game in the country; a passion that grows better when it is organic from the bottom rather than organised from the top.

after newsletter promotion

The national side is still a problem, though, and even for a fanbase well accustomed to disappointment the recent 5-0 defeat against Palestine at home, the fourth-biggest loss in history, was tough to take. As one journalist said, being thrashed by Brazil, Japan and Wales is one thing, but Palestine was another. There were some mitigating circumstances in that a number of national team players were at the Asian Games, where China actually performed well, losing narrowly against South Korea in the bronze final.

There are signs that the gap behind Korea is not as wide as it used to be. China reached the final of the under-17 and under-23 Asian championships this year before losing both against Japan. Compared with the rest of Asia’s best, young Chinese players are closing the gap at a technical and tactical level. Exporting more players to Europe is necessary to play at a higher level and if that happens, that senior national shirt may feel a little lighter.

Failure can, however, be hard to shake off as Chengdu Rongcheng may well find out if they mess this up.
